## Phase 1: Ward reads well on every phone

Today a phone gets only word lists and patterns (59% of Roman Urdu abuse caught) while a
computer with Gemma 4 gets 86%. The children with the least get the weakest Ward.

| Piece | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ward Lite model** | A small multilingual classifier (about 100 MB after int8), distilled from Gemma 4 and public datasets, run in the app with ONNX Runtime Web. Works on every platform, offline, in tens of milliseconds per message. | Beats the word lists on every language in the scorecard, using only data the scorecard never sees |
| **Training data without leakage** | Public train splits only (never the eval splits), plus synthetic kid-style chats in English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla written and labelled by Gemma 4, including friendly banter as hard negatives | A data card listing every source, split and count |
| **The safety gate** | The model can raise a message's severity, but never lowers one the word lists call dangerous; fixture chats keep their verdicts | Engine tests on every fixture |
| **Tiers** | Ward picks the strongest reader available: Gemma 4 (computer) > Gemma 3n on the phone > Ward Lite > word lists, and says which one read the chat | "How I worked this out" names the tier |
| **Gemma 4 E2B on capable phones** | A native Android plugin running Gemma 4 E2B through LiteRT-LM (2 GB, downloaded by choice, phones with 6 GB+ RAM) | Runs on the CI emulator; measured on a real phone |

**Phase 1 results (2026-10-29).** Ward Lite shipped: 37.7 MB, 8 ms per message, raise-only. On
the scorecard a phone now catches 85% of Roman Urdu abuse (word lists alone: 59%) and 83% of
English (10%); Bangla is at 39% (10%), and needs more real non-abusive Bangla chat. Gemma 4 E2B
scored about a third even with 5 messages per request, so it doesn't judge chats: on phones it
writes (the message to a trusted adult, feedback on lesson answers). Still to do: measure both
on a real low-end phone, and grow the Bangla data.

## Phase 2: every child can use it

| Piece | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Shared-phone mode** | Profiles on one device, each behind its own PIN; no message text in any preview; a quick-exit button | Two profiles on one phone can't see each other's checks, vault or progress |
| **Read-aloud** | On-device text-to-speech for every screen and lesson, Urdu included; voice input for written answers | Every lesson can be completed without reading |
| **Urdu UI** | Full interface in Urdu script with right-to-left layout, then Hindi, Bangla, Pashto, Sindhi, Punjabi (Shahmukhi) | All strings in translation files; no hard-coded English |
| **Quiet mode** | A neutral app name and icon, for children whose risk is at home | Only after a safeguarding reviewer signs off |

## Phase 3: the whole picture, not only the victim
| **Get help now** | Anything dangerous puts helplines for the child's country first (including Pakistan's Madadgaar 1098 and DRF Cyber Harassment Helpline 0800-39393), plus Take It Down for images. |
| **Evidence vault** | Saved chats are encrypted (AES-GCM, key from a PIN via PBKDF2), each message SHA-256 fingerprinted. |
| **Resilience Path** | Duolingo-style daily lessons with streaks and XP: *Spot it, Shut it down, Save it, Say it, Back them up, Lock it down, Bounce back*. Content per age band (8 to 10, 11 to 13, 14 to 17). No hearts to lose. |
| **Your night light** | Six looks the child picks from a gallery, no gender question. The age band changes how playful or grown-up it feels. |

### The child's circle

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **For the adult they told** | A page the child hands over, in English and Urdu: what to do in the first minutes, what not to do (take the phone away, confront the other family), and next steps with school, the app and a helpline. |
| **Class mode** | A teacher projects any lesson for a whole room: one question at a time, the class votes or talks, then the answer. Ground rules up front. Nothing recorded, no accounts. |

### The community

They get a readable page plus `ward-report.json` in a documented format ([docs/REPORT.md](docs/REPORT.md)) with a digest a helpline can check. Only hurtful messages go in. result.output:
## Phase 3: the whole picture, not only the victim

| Piece | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **"Was I mean?"** | A non-judgemental self-check for a child worried they went too far, leading to repair lessons | Content reviewed; never shames, never stores |
| **Help a friend** | "Checking for a friend" becomes a full upstander flow: how to reach out, what to say, how to bring in an adult without breaking trust | A complete path from check to action |
| **Stories** | Branching interactive stories with recurring characters that grow with the age bands | One story per unit per age band |
| **Lessons that respond** | After a check, Ward suggests the lessons that fit what happened; streaks never guilt-trip | Suggestions shown after checks |
| **Safety plan** | A teen safety plan (warning signs, things that help, people, safe places) kept in the vault, one tap from any urgent result | Reviewed by a professional before release |

## Phase 4: the circle and the community

| Piece | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Caseworker viewer** | A free, offline web page where a helpline opens `ward-report.json`, verifies the digest, reads the case and exports to intake | Opens and verifies any report Ward makes |
| **Counsellor mode** | A school counsellor's Ward that receives reports by file or QR, verifies them and keeps local case notes | No server anywhere |
| **School kit** | Printable lesson plans, a parent letter (English and Urdu), and an anonymous before/after class survey with a scoring sheet | A school can run a term and measure it alone |
| **One-click desktop** | Gemma bundled through llama.cpp inside the desktop app, no Ollama install; a lab mode that wipes itself for shared school computers | Fresh machine to first close read with one download |
| **Give Ward to a friend** | Share the app's own APK over Bluetooth or Nearby Share, no internet needed; Play Store and F-Droid listings | APK shared phone to phone in CI |

## Phase 5: proof and staying alive

| Piece | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ward Annotate** | Vetted teachers and youth volunteers label synthetic and public messages (never real children's chats) to grow the training data | First community-labelled release |
| **Red-team set** | Disguised insults, coded bullying and tricky banter, rerun on every release with the scorecard | Published per language, including failures |
| **"This is wrong"** | A correction button on every judgement; corrections stay on the device unless the child shares them | Shown on every flagged message |
| **Governance** | Safeguarding policy, language maintainers, youth advisory group, Digital Public Goods application | Policy published; application submitted |

## Phase 6: prevention at the keyboard

An opt-in Ward keyboard for Android that notices a hurtful message before it's sent and offers
a pause. Everything on the device, nothing logged. Built only after the safeguarding review in
Phase 5, because a keyboard sees everything a child types.

## Partner technologies
## Partner technologies

Ward's rule is that a child's messages never leave their device, so partner services are used to
**build, evaluate, host static content and keep instructions current**, never to read a chat.

| Partner | Where it helps Ward | Phase | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Gemma** | Everything that reads: Gemma 4 E4B on computers, Gemma 4 E2B on phones (LiteRT-LM), Gemma 4 as the teacher that writes and labels Ward Lite's training data, ShieldGemma as the baseline | 1 | In use |
| **ElevenLabs** | Read-aloud: lesson narration and the adult guide pre-recorded in English and Urdu, shipped as audio files inside the app (static text, no child data); Ward's voice for the youngest band | 2 | English shipped (107 clips); Urdu next |
| **DigitalOcean** | A GPU droplet for the heavy, data-free jobs: generating and labelling synthetic chats with Gemma 4 at scale, training a larger teacher before distilling, and rerunning the scorecard on every release | 1, 5 | Planned |
| **Render** | Hosting the static pieces: a try-it-in-the-browser demo (runs entirely client-side), the caseworker viewer, and the docs | 4 | Planned |
| **Browserbase + SerpApi** | A weekly job that finds the official report/block help pages for WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Discord and checks they still match the Coach's steps, opening an issue when an app changes its menus | 4 | Planned |
| **Entire** | Checkpoints of these agent sessions with the code, so how Ward was built can be audited and replayed | All | To enable |
| **Auth0 for AI Agents** | Logins for vetted Ward Annotate volunteers (adults only, synthetic and public data only) | 5 | Later |
| **Tiger Data** | Scorecard and red-team history across releases, so regressions in any language are visible | 5 | Later |
| **Temporal** | Making the distillation pipeline (generate, label, leak-check, train, gate, export) durable and resumable when it runs for hours on a GPU droplet | 5 | Later |

Not used, on purpose: services that would store or process a child's chats or memories in the
cloud. Tinker would have fit Phase 1 fine-tuning, but credits ran out; Ward Lite trains on a
laptop instead (an M-series Mac fine-tunes it in minutes).

content.text:
Phase 3 is pushed to main (`c4f11ae`). Four of its five pieces are built, in English and Urdu, and none of it needed credits. The push also published the 12 Entire checkpoints.

- **Lessons that respond:** results and coach screens now end with up to three lessons chosen from what Ward found. For example, the example chat checked for a friend suggests "Be the first one", the photo-pressure lesson and "What's safe to share".
- **Help a friend:** a check done "for a friend" now gets its own coach. It covers:
  - a private message to them, with three lines to copy
  - not joining in or fighting back
  - keeping the proof and reporting anonymously
  - bringing in an adult without going behind their back. If the friend is in danger, it says to tell an adult today even if they asked not to.
- **"Was I mean?":** five private questions, with nothing saved and never the word "bully".
  - The answers lead either to reassurance or to five repair steps, with apologies to copy.
  - If the child's own messages in a chat look harsh, the result now mentions it gently and links here.
- **Safety plan (ages 14 to 17):** five short sections with tap-to-add ideas, locked in the vault under the same PIN and saved as they type. The country's helplines sit below. I confirmed only encrypted text is stored, a wrong PIN can't open it, and it stays out of the evidence list.
  - It still needs a professional's review before it's opened to everyone, as the phase plan says. `docs/PHASES.md` records that.

Testing caught a real bug: the vault never closed its database connections, so "delete everything" on a shared phone left the data in place until the app restarted. That's fixed and retested.

content.text: Now the viewer itself. All report content goes in through `textContent`, never as HTML, since a report file is untrusted input. Times are shown in the caseworker's time zone, and the page says so.

input.content:
Ward case viewer

Works offline. Nothing you open here leaves this computer.

Drop a ward-report.json here

A child makes this file in Ward and chooses to give it to you. This page checks that the messages weren't edited after they were saved, then lays out the case.

What the checks prove, and what they don't

The digest is SHA-256 over the conversation facts and every incident. If any message, time, name or count in this file was changed after Ward made it, the digest won't match.

Each message's fingerprint is SHA-256 of sender, time and text, taken when the child saved the chat in Ward's locked vault. A match means that message is exactly as saved.

What neither proves: that the chat export itself was genuine. If it matters, ask the child to show you the conversation in the app. Times come from the child's chat export and are shown in this computer's time zone.

Only hurtful messages from others are in a report. The rest of the chat, the child's own messages, and anyone who stood up for them stay on the child's phone.

The caseworker viewer is built and pushed (`5ae9872`), and CI passed. All 24 tests pass: 15 engine, 5 lessons, 4 viewer.

**What it is:** [`viewer/ward-viewer.html`](viewer/ward-viewer.html), a single file a helpline saves and double-clicks. It has no dependencies and works fully offline, and its content-security policy blocks every network request, so nothing opened in it can be uploaded. It also ships inside every Ward build as `ward-viewer.html`, and the child's report page now tells helplines where to find it.

**What it does:**
- **Checks the report.** It recomputes the digest and every message's fingerprint. When something was edited, it says so at the top and marks exactly which message changed. With the sample I edited message 3; only that row showed "✗ Changed", and the banner said the report was altered.
- **Lays out the case in intake order.**
  - The child's own answer on whether they're in danger now, Ward's reading, and the dangerous categories.
  - What the child wants, and only the details they chose to share.
  - The conversation facts, then each account (including ones added to the group that only attacked) and the patterns.
  - Every hurtful message with its fingerprint status.
- **Exports** a plain-text case summary to copy, a CSV for intake systems and a print view. The CSV has Excel's UTF-8 marker for Urdu, and a message that starts like a formula (such as `=HYPERLINK(...)`) is kept as plain text.
- **Includes a sample report**, built from the engine's own test chat, for trying it out or demoing.

**Tested:**
- An automated test runs the viewer's own check code against reports the engine builds, one untouched and three tampered (an edited message, a changed count, a removed message). That test now runs in CI.
- In the browser:
  - A message carrying an HTML payload rendered as plain text, and nothing ran.
  - The CSV downloads correctly with the network block in place.
  - There were no console errors.

Inside the in-app browser, a file opened from disk loads in a restricted mode where the check can't run. The viewer then explains how to open it properly. A normally double-clicked file in Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari runs the check fine.

The rest of Phase 4 (counsellor mode, school kit, one-click desktop, sharing the APK phone to phone) and branching stories from Phase 3 aren't built yet.

content.text:
Branching stories are built and pushed (`05a9c0e`). All 28 tests pass: 15 engine, 9 lessons, 4 viewer.

**The stories**, one per age band, in English and Urdu, using the lessons' characters:
- **Mia's drawing (ages 8–10, Back them up):** the class chat laughs at Mia's drawing. You can laugh along, stay quiet, or say "I like it". Each choice leads on to messaging Mia privately, telling a teacher or saying sorry.
- **The secret fan (11–13, Shut it down):** an anonymous account messages *you*. You can reply angrily, keep reading, or screenshot, block and report, then tell Zara or Ammi.
- **The screenshot (14–17, Lock it down):** Hamza screenshots Zara's close-friends story and asks you to forward it. The choices include whether to keep Zara's promise not to tell an adult while it spreads.

**How a story plays:**
- Lines arrive one at a time, like a real chat, then you choose. The reader is never named or gendered.
- Endings are kind, mixed or hard, never a telling-off. Each says what the choice did and what else could still help.
- "Try a different choice" restarts the story, and the ending shows "2 of 3 endings found".
- The first ending of a story earns 10 XP and keeps the streak, like a lesson.
- Stories sit on the Path after their unit and are never locked.

**Checks:**
- **Tests:** they walk every path in every story (no dead links, no loops, at least one kind ending each). They also check the reader is never gendered and the Urdu matches the English structure exactly.
- **In the browser:** I played routes in English and Urdu, on desktop and phone width, and the XP and ending counts came out right.
- **Two bugs found and fixed while testing:**
  - The whole app crashed on opening a story. Newer browsers return a Promise from the scroll call, and React took it for a cleanup function.
  - Picking a choice could show and count an ending before its lines had played, which lost the XP label.

**The Urdu translation:** a subagent did it. It also caught two mistakes in my English, now fixed:
- Mia replied "please don't take it off" to her own drawing.
- "send it to the boys gc" implied the reader is a boy.

A native Urdu speaker should still read the stories.

The goal of one story per unit per age band needs 18 more. Each is about an hour of writing plus translation.

The question isn't "is the classifier accurate" but "are children better off".

### Stage 1: feasibility pilot (3 to 5 schools, one city, one school term)

A pilot this size can't detect an effect of g = 0.15; it isn't meant to. It answers whether the
thing is used, safe, and worth a proper trial.

| Question | Measure | Go if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Do teachers run it? | Class-mode lessons taught per class, from the teacher's own log | 4+ lessons per class per term |
| Do children use it? | Anonymous end-of-term survey: "Did you use Ward? Which parts?" | 30%+ of students used it at least once |
| Does it get children to tell someone? | Survey: "The last time something mean happened online, did you tell an adult?" before and after | Rises from baseline |
| Is it safe? | Every report of distress, misuse (e.g. a parent using it to read chats) or a wrong "looks okay", logged by the school counsellor | No serious harm; every case reviewed within a week |
| Do helplines find the report useful? | Caseworker rating of 20+ Ward reports against their usual intake | Faster or more complete intake |

### Stage 2: controlled trial (2027 to 2028)

Cluster-randomised by school, comparing schools with Ward (child app plus class mode plus adult
guide) to schools on the waiting list. Primary outcomes: cyber-victimisation and
cyber-perpetration on a validated scale such as the European Cyberbullying Intervention Project
Questionnaire (ECIPQ), at baseline, 3 and 9 months. Secondary: help-seeking, wellbeing, bystander
intervention. Sample size from a power calculation with an expected effect near the
meta-analytic g = 0.13 to 0.18; that means thousands of students across dozens of schools, which
is why stage 1 has to earn it.

### How we measure without breaking the promise

Nothing is collected from a child's phone. Outcomes come from anonymous school surveys run by the
school, the teacher's own log of lessons taught, and helpline caseworkers' ratings of reports
they received. If the app ever counts anything (lessons finished, checks run), it stays on the
device and is only shared if the child chooses to show it.

## Staged path to 2030

| When | What | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Now to 3 months | Shared-phone mode, Urdu script, distilled phone model, safeguarding review, report co-designed with one helpline | A helpline and one school agree to pilot |
| 3 to 12 months | Stage 1 pilot in one city; publish results, good or bad | Go/no-go on the table above |
| Year 2 to 3 | Stage 2 trial; second country through a partner (a child helpline or education NGO) | Published trial results |
| To 2030 | Free public good adopted through school systems and child helplines; languages added by maintainers; Ward report accepted by helplines and platforms as an intake format | Used in schools in 3+ countries, maintained by people who aren't us |

## Staying alive

- **Open and public.** MIT licence. Apply to the Digital Public Goods Alliance registry: its
  standard expects safeguards for underage users, which is what Ward is built around.

content.text:
The school kit is built and pushed (`712169b`), and CI passed. It's under Me, then "Teach a class", then School kit, in English and Urdu. Nothing in it collects data about any child.

**What's in it:**
- **Term plan:** nine weeks for the chosen age band. Week 0 is the letter home and the "before" survey, weeks 1 to 7 cover one unit each, and week 8 is the "after" survey.
- **Lesson plans:** one 25-minute plan per unit, built from the actual lessons. Each has:
  - the aim and a warm-up question
  - the lessons to show in class mode
  - two talk questions
  - a close that names the country's helplines (Madadgaar 1098 and DRF 0800-39393 in Pakistan)
  - five steps for what to do if a child tells you something
- **Letter home:** the teacher fills in the school, class, their name and contact, then prints it in English, Urdu or both. It explains Ward's privacy plainly, warns parents not to take the child's phone away, and points to the guide for adults.
- **Anonymous survey:** the same questions before and after, matching the pilot measures in `docs/ROADMAP.md`:
  - in the last month, being picked on, being mean, seeing it happen, and telling an adult
  - six "how true is this" statements about confidence
  - after only, whether they used Ward and which parts
- **Results:**
  - The teacher counts the paper sheets and types in totals. The page shows each question before and after, with the change in green or red.
  - It knows that fewer children being picked on is better.
  - It leaves "nothing happened" out of the telling-an-adult rate.
  - It warns not to share results from rounds under 10 sheets, since they could identify children.
  - It includes a lesson log, and downloads a CSV with totals only.

Each part prints on its own, black on white, with right-to-left layout for Urdu.

**Checked:**
- In the browser: the class results maths (10 of 24 → 5 of 22 shows 42% → 23%, −19 points, marked better), the small-class warning, the print frame with both languages and a page break, and the letter filled in both languages.
- A new scoring test, now in CI. That makes 30 tests in total.
- I caught one bug before testing: the tally inputs would have lost focus on every keystroke.

**Not checked:**
- An actual printed page or PDF. I confirmed what goes to the printer, not the paper output.
- Printing on Android. Its web view often ignores print requests, but teachers will mostly use a computer.

The Urdu translation was again done by a subagent, and its review caught three things I fixed:
- The kit called the class screen "Class mode", but in the app it's "Teach a class".
- The percentage captions read awkwardly.
- Safeguarding now says "safeguarding lead or head teacher", since many Pakistani schools don't have a safeguarding lead.
Counsellor mode

Here's the plan. Counsellor mode lives in the app under the adults section, so there's still no server.

- **Receiving reports:** by file (`ward-report.json`), or by QR from the child's phone, for when there's no cable, email or internet. A report is 5–20 KB, too big for one QR code. So the child's phone compresses it and shows a short looping sequence of codes, and the counsellor's camera collects them all.
- **Checking:** every report is verified the same way as the case viewer: the digest plus each message's fingerprint. I'll move that check into the engine so the app and viewer share one implementation.
- **Cases:** each case gets a status (new, ongoing, closed) and dated notes. They're encrypted in the counsellor's own vault under their vault PIN, since case notes about children are sensitive.

First the report dialog, to see how reports are made and saved today:

content.text:
Counsellor mode is built and pushed (`2bad99f`). CI, the Android build and all four desktop builds now pass (`08e3c3e`), with 35 tests passing (16 engine, 9 lessons, 10 app and viewer).

**What it does:** it's under Me, then Counsellor mode, in English and Urdu, for a school counsellor or any trusted adult. There's no server anywhere.

- **Receiving a report:**
  - **As a file:** the counsellor opens the `ward-report.json` the child shared.
  - **By QR:** after making a report, the child's phone now offers "Save or share the files" or "Give it by QR". The QR option compresses the report and shows it as a looping set of codes, six for the sample report. The counsellor's camera collects them in any order, with a progress bar, and no internet is needed either side.
- **Checking:** every report gets the digest check plus each message's fingerprint, now shared in the engine. Edited messages are marked one by one.
- **Cases:** each has a status (new, ongoing, closed; the first note moves it to ongoing) and dated notes. They're encrypted in the vault under the counsellor's PIN, and a case can be printed.
- **Permissions:** the desktop app now refuses every permission except the camera (video only). Android asks for the camera only when scanning, and the Mac app explains why it needs it.

**Checked:**
- Every QR frame, rendered as an image, decodes with the same decoder the scanner uses.
- Full scan in the browser: the real scanner read the six-part loop from a stand-in camera and saved a verified case marked "by QR".
- Files: the sample, a tampered copy, a duplicate and a non-report file each gave the right result.
- Notes survive re-locking, a wrong PIN is refused, and only ciphertext is stored.

**Bugs found and fixed:**
- **A tampered copy was hidden behind the genuine case.** I first keyed cases by the digest stored in the file, which an edit doesn't change, so an edited report opened the original instead. Cases are now keyed by their full content, so an edited copy shows up separately and flagged.
- **A non-report file got the wrong message,** saying it came from an unsupported version of Ward.
- **Every desktop build had been failing since Phase 2.** The smoke test looked for the word "Ward" on the first screen, but a fresh install now opens on the language picker. It now checks that a screen rendered.

**Not tested:** two real phones scanning each other. The browser pane blocks the camera, so I used a stand-in. It's worth one try with two phones before relying on QR.

**A gap in the report format:** the digest covers the messages and conversation facts, not the child's own answers ("in danger now", what they want, their details). Those could be edited without the check noticing. That's not evidence tampering, but a caseworker relies on "in danger now". Fixing it means a new format version (`ward.report/v2`), while keeping today's reports readable.

input.recap: Reports are now ward.report/v2, and the digest covers the child's own answers: in danger now, what they want, who the report is for and their details. Older v1 reports still open and check. Pushed as c4bae2e; CI passes, and all 39 tests pass locally.

content.text:
Reports now use a new format version, `ward.report/v2`, and its digest covers the child's own answers. Before, the check covered only the messages and conversation facts, so someone could change "in danger now" from yes to no and the check wouldn't notice. Now changing any of these makes the digest fail:

- "in danger now"
- what the child wants
- who the report is for
- the child's details
- the safety reading
- the accounts and patterns
- the time the evidence was saved

The digest takes these fields in a fixed order, so a system that reorders the top-level fields of the file doesn't break it.

**Older reports:** Ward, counsellor mode and the case viewer still open and check v1 reports. They now show a line saying the check covers the messages but not the child's answers, and that those should be confirmed with the child. [docs/REPORT.md](docs/REPORT.md) explains both versions and how to check one by hand.

**Tested:**
- **Automated tests:** all 39 pass. New tests change each of the child's answers one at a time and confirm each change is caught, in both the app's check and the case viewer's. They also confirm that reordering the fields still passes and that a v1 report still checks.
- **In the browser:** the regenerated sample report shows as unchanged. A copy with only "in danger now" changed shows "This report was changed after Ward made it". A v1 copy opens with the older-report line.
- **CI** passes on `c4bae2e`. The Android and desktop builds didn't run for this commit, so they're still last confirmed on the previous one.

**Not tested:** I didn't open counsellor mode in the app itself, because it needs the PIN. The new line there is a one-line condition; it type-checks and the app builds.

**Phase 1 results (2026-10-29).** Ward Lite shipped: 37.7 MB, 8 ms per message, raise-only. On
the scorecard a phone now catches 85% of Roman Urdu abuse (word lists alone: 59%) and 83% of
English (10%); Bangla is at 39% (10%), and needs more real non-abusive Bangla chat. Gemma 4 E2B
scored about a third even with 5 messages per request, so it doesn't judge chats: on phones it
writes (the message to a trusted adult, feedback on lesson answers). Still to do: measure both
on a real low-end phone, and grow the Bangla data.

**Phase 2 results (2026-10-29).** Shared-phone mode shipped: profiles with their own progress,
settings and vault database, an optional PIN (salted PBKDF2 hash), and quick exit from every
screen (a button, or Escape twice) that locks Ward and, on Android, sends it to the background;
the window is FLAG_SECURE so it never shows in the recents preview. The whole interface and all
seven units of lessons are in Urdu, right to left, in Noto Nastaliq Urdu, with Gemma writing its
notes in Urdu too. Read-aloud is on by default for the youngest band: 107 English lines
(onboarding, verdicts, coach steps, every lesson prompt and explanation) are recorded with
ElevenLabs and bundled offline; Urdu uses the device's Urdu voice for now. Still to do: record
the Urdu clips (about 9,000 characters; the script and voice are chosen), voice input for
written answers, a native Urdu speaker's review, and the next languages.

**Phase 3 progress (2026-10-29).** Four of five pieces shipped, in English and Urdu:
- **Lessons that respond:** every result and coach screen ends with up to three lessons chosen
  from what Ward found (exclusion, a pile-on, photo pressure, late nights, a friend's chat),
  for the child's age, new ones first. No streak pressure.
## Phase 6: prevention at the keyboard

An opt-in Ward keyboard for Android that notices a hurtful message before it's sent and offers
a pause. Everything on the device, nothing logged. Built only after the safeguarding review in
Phase 5, because a keyboard sees everything a child types.

content.text:
Ward has most of Phases 1–4 built and on main, but the DEV post doesn't exist yet. That matters more than any feature left, because the writing is weighted most heavily and nothing counts until it's published.

**Deadline:** the Week 4 page says submissions are due **today, 31 October, at 11:59 PM PDT**. That's 06:59 UTC on 1 November, about 18 hours from now. But DEV's own end time for the challenge reads as 06:59 UTC on *31 October*, six hours ago, and earlier weeks had the same one-day mismatch. Check the challenge page now. If the earlier time is right, the window has already closed.

**Where each phase stands**

| Phase | Status |
|---|---|
| **1. Reads well on every phone** | Done. Ward Lite is 37.7 MB and takes 8 ms per message, catching 85% of Roman Urdu and 83% of English abuse on the scorecard. Gemma 4 is used on computers, and on phones only to write. Not yet measured on a real low-end phone; Bangla is weak at 39%. |
| **2. Every child can use it** | Mostly done: shared-phone profiles with quick exit, the full Urdu interface, and English read-aloud (107 ElevenLabs clips). Urdu read-aloud uses the phone's own voice because the credits ran out. Not done: voice input, quiet mode (needs a safeguarding review first), and more languages. |
| **3. The whole picture** | Done: "Was I mean?", Help a friend, lessons suggested from what Ward found, the teen safety plan, and branching stories (one per age band; the goal is one per unit, so 18 more). |
| **4. The circle and the community** | 3 of 5 done: the caseworker viewer, the school kit and counsellor mode with QR transfer. The report format is now v2, so its check covers the child's own answers. Not started: "Give Ward to a friend" (sharing the app phone to phone) and one-click desktop (Gemma bundled inside the app). |
| **5. Proof and staying alive** | Not started: community labelling, a red-team set, a "This is wrong" button, governance. |
| **6. Keyboard** | Not started. It waits on the Phase 5 safeguarding review on purpose. |

**Health:** CI passes, the Android build launches on the emulator, and all four desktop installers build. All 39 tests pass.

**Still open outside the code**
- **The DEV post:** this is the critical path. It needs the #hf26challenge tag and the submission template. It should also cover how Ward fits the "Ghost in the Machine" theme (Ward's friendly ghost) and why open models matter here: children's chats never leave the phone.
- **Partner prize categories:** Ward has a real case for Gemma, ElevenLabs and Entire. Render, DigitalOcean, SerpApi and Browserbase are only planned, so they shouldn't be claimed.
- **Demo:** screenshots or a short film. The launch film was never made.
- **Release signing:** you still need to run the four `gh secret set` commands.
- **Testing:** QR scanning between two real phones hasn't been tried, and a native Urdu speaker hasn't reviewed the Urdu.

I'd stop building features and write the post now. I'll draft it as an unpublished draft for you to review, and nothing goes live without your yes.

input.description: More branching stories EN+UR
input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, a Hacktoberfest entry due in about 16 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. It's a pnpm monorepo: packages/engine (chat analysis), packages/lessons (lesson units and branching stories), apps/web (React 19 + Vite + Tailwind 4; the story player is apps/web/src/screens/Story.tsx), plus desktop, mobile, viewer, eval, train and docs. Read docs/PHASES.md (Phase 3, "Stories") first.

YOUR TASK: write more branching interactive stories, in English and Urdu. The goal in PHASES.md is one story per unit per age band; three exist today (mias-drawing for ages 8, secret-fan for 11, the-screenshot for 14) in packages/lessons/src/stories.ts and stories.ur.ts. Read packages/lessons/src/types.ts (Story, StoryScene, StoryChoice, StoryEnding with tone kind|mixed|hard, StoryLine with from?/me?), units.ts (which units exist for which band, and each unit's id), index.ts (storiesFor, storyById) and stories.test.ts (it walks every path, checks the reader is never gendered, and checks Urdu parity).

Write at least six new stories (two per age band: 8, 11, 14), each tied to a different unit than the existing story in that band. If time and quality allow, keep going towards one per unit per band. Quality matters more than count: a judge will play these.

Content rules (safeguarding; follow them exactly):
- Realistic chats and situations kids actually meet online: group chats, gaming, class groups, photos, nicknames, being left out, rumours, someone new being targeted, being the one who went too far. Recurring characters are good: reuse names from existing stories where it fits.
- Never preachy. Choices should be genuinely tempting both ways. Kind endings model concrete actions: checking on the person privately, not forwarding, saving evidence, blocking and reporting, telling a trusted adult. Hard endings show consequences honestly without gore, humiliation spectacle or despair.
- No self-harm method details, no sexual content. For the 14 band you may touch image-sharing pressure or threats, but carefully and ending with where to get help.
- The reader ("me" lines and choices) must never be gendered, in either language. Other characters can be.
- Urdu (stories.ur.ts) is in Urdu script, natural not literal. The child's own lines must be gender-neutral: avoid کرتا/کرتی, گیا/گئی, رہا/رہی after میں; use نے-constructions or the subjunctive. Chat lines between kids can use Roman Urdu where that's how kids actually text, matching the existing stories' style.
- Names: a mix of South Asian and global names, as the existing stories do.

Only touch packages/lessons/src/stories.ts, stories.ur.ts and, if genuinely needed, stories.test.ts. Don't touch docs/PHASES.md or README.md (the lead updates those).

Before finishing: run `pnpm test` from the repo root and `cd apps/web && npx tsc --noEmit -p .`; both must pass. Commit on your worktree branch with a clear message ending with the line:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge into main.

Report back: the branch name, each story (id, band, unit, one-line premise, its endings), what you tested, and any line you're unsure about in Urdu so a native speaker can check it.

input.description: "This is wrong" correction button
input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, a Hacktoberfest entry due in about 16 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. It's a pnpm monorepo: packages/engine (chat parsing and analysis; findings have severity 0-3 and categories), apps/web (React 19, Vite, Tailwind 4, Motion, Phosphor icons; i18n in apps/web/src/i18n/en.ts and ur.ts, where `ur: Dict` must match en's shape; `useT()` hook), plus desktop, mobile, viewer, eval, train, docs. Read docs/PHASES.md (Phase 5, '"This is wrong"') and README.md first.

YOUR TASK: build the '"This is wrong"' correction control (Phase 5): "A correction button on every judgement; corrections stay on the device unless the child shares them."

What it should do:
- On every flagged message in the result screen (apps/web/src/screens/Result.tsx; find where findings/messages are rendered), a small, calm control lets the child say Ward got it wrong: e.g. "It wasn't mean (a joke between friends)", "It was worse than Ward said", "Wrong kind of hurtful". Keep it light and non-intrusive; it must not clutter the result.
- The correction changes what the child sees for that message on that result (e.g. it's marked as "You said this was okay"), and is remembered on the device for that chat.
- SAFETY GATE (non-negotiable): a correction can never hide the help for dangerous messages (severity 3, or categories threat/selfharm/sexual/exposure). If the child marks one of those as "not mean", Ward thanks them, keeps the safety resources and the urgent framing visible, and says gently why. The engine's own verdict is never silently lowered for reports either: reports (packages/engine/src/report.ts, apps/web/src/lib/report.ts) are not changed by corrections.
- Privacy: corrections never leave the device. Read apps/web/src/lib/vault.ts and store.ts and choose where they live. If you store message text, it must be in the encrypted vault (the vault has special rows like `__plan` and the `case:` prefix that `list()` skips; follow that pattern), otherwise store only the message fingerprint (fingerprintMessages in the engine) plus the correction. Prefer the option that works when the vault isn't unlocked, without storing text in the clear.
- Sharing (optional for the child, opt-in): a "Help make Ward better" way to export corrections as a small JSON file the child can choose to send to the project. It must show exactly what will be shared before export and include message text only if the child ticks a box. No network calls at all; it's a file the child saves or shares, like the existing report export (look at how ReportDialog / exportReport do it).
- All strings in en.ts and ur.ts. Urdu rule: the child's own lines must be gender-neutral (avoid کرتا/کرتی, گیا/گئی, رہا/رہی after میں; use نے-constructions or the subjunctive); Ward's own voice is masculine. RTL via logical classes (ms-, me-, ps-, pe-, start-, end-) and `.flip-rtl` on directional icons.
- Match the surrounding code's style and comment density; reuse existing components in apps/web/src/components/ui.tsx.
- Add a focused test where logic is non-trivial (e.g. the safety gate), runnable with `node --test --experimental-strip-types`, and add it to the root package.json "test" script.

Don't touch docs/PHASES.md or README.md (the lead updates those). Avoid packages/lessons and desktop/mobile.

Verify in a browser: the dev server is `pnpm dev` (Vite). Use the Browser preview tools if available to load the app, run a check on the sample chat, mark messages wrong (including a dangerous one), reload and confirm it's remembered, and check Urdu (RTL) and a mobile width. If you can't run a browser, say so.

Before finishing: `pnpm test`, `cd apps/web && npx tsc --noEmit -p .` and `pnpm --filter @ward/web build` must pass. Commit on your worktree branch with clear messages ending with the line:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge into main.

Report back: the branch name, commits, files touched, the design you chose (where corrections are stored and why), what you tested and how, what's not done, and any decision the user should confirm.

input.description: Red-team set and scorecard
input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, a Hacktoberfest entry due in about 16 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. It's a pnpm monorepo: packages/engine (chat parsing and analysis: word lists/slang packs per language plus an optional small classifier, "Ward Lite", run raise-only), eval/ (the scorecard: eval/run.ts, eval/data.ts, eval/data, eval/results), train/ (how Ward Lite was trained: train/README.md, train/DATA.md, build-data.ts), apps/web, docs. Read docs/PHASES.md (Phase 1 results and Phase 5 "Red-team set"), train/DATA.md and eval/run.ts first.

YOUR TASK: build Ward's red-team set (Phase 5): "Disguised insults, coded bullying and tricky banter, rerun on every release with the scorecard. Published per language, including failures."

1. Write a red-team set by hand (synthetic only: never real children's messages, never scraped chats) covering English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla (Bangla script and romanised), the languages Ward reads. Categories to cover, each with hurtful items AND look-alike harmless items:
   - spelling disguises: leetspeak, spacing (m o t i), repeated letters, emoji stand-ins, mixed scripts
   - coded and new slang, initialisms
   - sarcasm and backhanded compliments
   - exclusion said politely ("we'll make a new group without...")
   - threats and self-harm urging phrased indirectly (keep it non-graphic)
   - hard negatives: friendly banter between friends, reclaimed words, a child quoting what was said to them while asking for help, gaming trash talk that isn't targeted
   Aim for roughly 40 to 80 items per language, each with a label (hurtful severity 0-3 and category, matching the engine's types in packages/engine/src/types.ts) and a short note on what it tests.
2. Keep it out of training. Put it under eval/redteam/ (or the eval layout's convention), and add a check (a test in the root `pnpm test`, or in train's build step) that fails if any red-team text appears in train/data or the training build inputs. Document in train/DATA.md that train/ must never read eval/redteam.
3. A runner that scores the red-team set the same way eval/run.ts scores the scorecard (word lists alone, and with Ward Lite where eval/run.ts can run it in Node), per language and per category, and writes results (eval/results or similar) plus a human-readable docs/REDTEAM.md: method, per-language tables, and the failures listed honestly (a sample of misses and false alarms with why). Add an npm script, e.g. "redteam".
4. Do NOT tune the engine against this set (that would overfit and make the published numbers meaningless). Report only. If you see an obvious engine bug (not a tuning question), describe it in your report instead of fixing it.

Rules: the content is safeguarding-sensitive. Keep hurtful items realistic but not gratuitous; no sexual content involving minors beyond the minimal label-able phrasing of pressure ("send pics"), no self-harm methods. Don't touch docs/PHASES.md or README.md (the lead updates those). Don't touch apps/web.

Before finishing: `pnpm test` must pass, and the runner must run end to end. Commit on your worktree branch with clear messages ending with the line:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge into main.

Report back: the branch name, counts per language and category, the headline results (word lists vs Ward Lite per language), the worst failure classes, files touched, and anything the user should decide.

input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, a Hacktoberfest entry due in about 16 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. Read docs/PHASES.md (Phase 4, "Give Ward to a friend") and README.md first, then look at the existing native Android plugins in mobile/android/app/src/main/java to follow their pattern.

YOUR TASK: "Give Ward to a friend": share the app's own APK phone to phone with no internet (Bluetooth, Nearby Share/Quick Share, or any share target), for kids in places where the Play Store is hard to use.

1. Android: a small Capacitor plugin that copies the installed APK (getApplicationInfo().sourceDir; handle split APKs sensibly — if the install is split, say so and fall back to the release link) into the cache dir with a clear file name (e.g. Ward-<version>.apk), and opens the system share sheet via a FileProvider with type application/vnd.android.package-archive. Also expose the APK's SHA-256 and the signing certificate's SHA-256 so the friend can check it's the real Ward. Register the FileProvider in AndroidManifest.xml with the narrowest path config.

input.description: One-click desktop with llama.cpp
input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, a Hacktoberfest entry due in about 16 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. It's a pnpm monorepo: apps/web (React 19 + Vite; the web app, which the desktop and Android apps wrap), desktop/ (Electron: desktop/main.mjs serves the web build over an `app://` protocol, has a WARD_SMOKE smoke test used by CI, and a permission handler that only allows the camera), packages/engine, .github/workflows (a desktop workflow builds installers on mac-arm64, mac-x64, windows-x64 and linux-x64 with electron-builder and runs the smoke test). Today, on a computer, Ward uses Gemma 4 through a local Ollama install if the user has one; find exactly how in apps/web/src/lib (run.ts and related) and desktop/main.mjs. Read docs/PHASES.md (Phase 1 tiers, Phase 4 "One-click desktop") and README.md first.

YOUR TASK: "One-click desktop": "Gemma bundled through llama.cpp inside the desktop app, no Ollama install; a lab mode that wipes itself for shared school computers. Done when: fresh machine to first close read with one download."

1. llama.cpp in the desktop app: use node-llama-cpp (it ships prebuilt llama.cpp binaries for mac/win/linux, Metal/CPU/Vulkan) in Electron's main process. Check its current docs for Electron packaging (asarUnpack, which binaries to include per platform) and pin an exact, released version. Do not put the model in the installer.
2. Model download with consent: on first use (or from a settings button), the app explains, shows the size, and downloads a Gemma 4 GGUF (pick the small instruct model Ward uses on computers, E4B, or E2B if that is the right size/quality tradeoff; find an official or well-known GGUF on Hugging Face, e.g. ggml-org or unsloth, quantised around Q4) into Electron's userData, with progress, resume or retry, and a SHA-256 check against a pinned hash. The download is the only network request and carries no child data. Respect the existing CSP and permission handler; any network for the download happens in the main process.
3. Wire it to the app: the renderer must use bundled Gemma exactly where it would use Ollama today, through the narrowest bridge (an IPC exposed via a preload with contextIsolation, or an Ollama-compatible endpoint on 127.0.0.1 with a random port and token; choose one and explain). Preference order for computers: an existing Ollama with Gemma 4 > bundled llama.cpp Gemma > Ward Lite > word lists, and the app's "How I worked this out" should name which one read the chat (look at how tiers are reported today).
4. Lab mode for shared school computers: a setting (and a command-line flag, e.g. --lab) where Ward keeps nothing between sessions: all storage (IndexedDB, localStorage, caches) is cleared on quit and on launch, with a clear banner saying so. The downloaded model may stay.
5. CI must stay green on all four platforms, including the WARD_SMOKE test. Keep installer size growth reasonable and say what it is. If node-llama-cpp's native packaging can't be made to work on all four targets in time, do not ship it broken: make it degrade cleanly (feature hidden where the binary isn't present) and report exactly what fails.

Rules: match surrounding code style; contextIsolation on, nodeIntegration off; no secrets; don't touch docs/PHASES.md or README.md (the lead updates those). Strings shown in the web UI go in apps/web/src/i18n/en.ts and ur.ts (`ur: Dict` must match en's shape; Urdu child-facing lines gender-neutral, Ward's voice masculine; RTL via logical classes). Avoid packages/lessons and mobile/.

Test locally: `pnpm test`, `cd apps/web && npx tsc --noEmit -p .`, `pnpm --filter @ward/web build`, then build and run the desktop app on this Mac (see desktop/package.json scripts; WARD_SMOKE=1 for the smoke test). If you can, actually download the model and run one close read end to end on this Mac, and time it. Commit on your worktree branch with clear messages ending with the line:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge into main; the lead will push and watch the four-platform CI.

Report back: branch name, commits, files touched, the bridge design and why, the model file (repo, file, size, hash), installer size change, what you tested and timings, what's not done, and anything the user must decide.

input.description: Governance and safeguarding docs
input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo github.com/MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/ward, a Hacktoberfest entry). You are in a git worktree of the repo. Read README.md, docs/PHASES.md (especially Phase 5 "Governance"), docs/HARMS.md, docs/PLAN.md, docs/ROADMAP.md and docs/REPORT.md first so everything you write is true to what Ward actually does today.

YOUR TASK: draft Ward's governance documents (Phase 5: "Safeguarding policy, language maintainers, youth advisory group, Digital Public Goods application. Done when: policy published; application submitted"). You're drafting; a human safeguarding professional must review before any of it is final, and every document must say so at the top.

Write, as new files (do not edit existing docs):
1. docs/SAFEGUARDING.md: Ward's safeguarding policy. Principles (child-led, on-device, no data collection), age bands (8-10, 11-13, 14-17) and how content differs, what Ward does when it sees danger (how the app escalates, helplines, never contacting anyone on the child's behalf), how content (lessons, stories, coach steps) is written and reviewed, the gated features and why (quiet mode, the keyboard), handling of disclosures that reach the project (e.g. via GitHub issues or email), reporting concerns about the project itself, and what Ward will never do. Ground every claim in the code/docs; if something is aspirational, label it "planned".
2. docs/GOVERNANCE.md: how decisions are made, maintainer roles including per-language maintainers (what they own: slang packs, translations, lesson review), how someone becomes one, a youth advisory group with terms of reference that protect the young people in it (parental consent, no personal data published, adult moderators with safeguarding checks, paid or credited fairly), and a safeguarding lead role.
3. content.text:
Six agents are running in their own worktrees, so none of them touch main:

1. **More stories:** at least two new ones per age band, in English and Urdu.
2. **"This is wrong" button:** a child can correct Ward on any message, and the correction stays on the phone. It can never hide the help shown for dangerous messages.
3. **Red-team set:** disguised insults, coded bullying and harmless look-alikes in all four languages. It's scored and published with its failures, never used to tune Ward, and checked so it can't leak into training.
4. **Give Ward to a friend:** the Android app shares its own APK over Bluetooth or Nearby Share, with a fingerprint the friend can check. Web and desktop get a QR code to the download page instead.
5. **One-click desktop:** Gemma runs inside the desktop app through llama.cpp, so there's no Ollama to install. The model downloads only after you agree, and a lab mode wipes everything on shared school computers.
6. **Governance drafts:** a safeguarding policy, governance, a code of conduct, a security policy and a draft Digital Public Goods application. Each is marked as needing review by a safeguarding professional.

I'm holding three things back on purpose:
- **Quiet mode and the keyboard:** the plan says both wait for a safeguarding review.
- **Voice input:** it's a privacy choice, so it's in the questions below.
- **Bangla data and real-phone timings:** these need a device or compute I don't have.

**The Discord idea: Ward as a friendly ghost in Discord**

Discord's minimum age is 13, so this is for Ward's 14–17 band and maybe the 11–13 band, and it matches the "Ghost in the Machine" theme.

1. **"Check with Ward", a right-click on any message.** A teen adds Ward to their own account, so it works in any server or DM, even ones that never added the bot. Ward reads only the message they pick, and only they see its reply:
   - Ward's verdict and why
   - what to do on Discord (block, mute, Discord's own report flow, leave the server)
   - a "Save as evidence" button

   Ward doesn't need extra Discord permissions to read the message the teen picks.
2. **Evidence without a database.** Each saved message is fingerprinted and sent to the teen as a DM from Ward. Later, `/ward report` builds a `ward.report/v2` from those DMs. Counsellor mode, the case viewer and helplines can already open and check that file. Ward's server keeps nothing: the teen's own DMs are the storage.
3. **`/ward help`:** helplines for the teen's region, which Ward already has, plus Discord's safety links.
4. **Optional server mode, for moderators of teen communities:**
   - dangerous messages (threats, urging self-harm, sharing private photos) go privately to a mods channel
   - the targeted member gets a quiet DM offering support
   - the sender gets a private "that might land hard, edit or delete?", the same pause-before-you-send idea as the planned keyboard

   It never punishes anyone automatically. This needs Discord's Message Content permission, which Discord makes servers opt into.

**Why open matters here:** the bot runs the same open engine and Ward Lite model as the app, on the CPU, in milliseconds. No closed moderation API sees what teens send. A school or a server can read the code and run it on their own machine. Gemma can be added if the host has it.

**Being honest about privacy:** unlike the app, the bot does run on someone's server. Discord already carries the message, and the bot reads only what's selected, logs nothing and stores nothing, but the post will have to say this plainly.

**What you'll need to do:** create the app in Discord's Developer Portal and put its token in a local `.env` file yourself. I can't create accounts or handle tokens. I'll give you the exact steps.

# Ward Lite

A small multilingual classifier that reads chat messages on any device, including cheap phones
with no internet. It's `intfloat/multilingual-e5-small` fine-tuned with two outputs per message,
**hurtful** and **danger** (threats, telling someone to hurt themselves, sexual pressure, threats
to expose), then trimmed to the vocabulary our languages use and quantised to int8 ONNX.

In the app it has **raise-only** authority: it can flag what the word lists missed, but it can
never clear a warning. Only Gemma 4 on a computer may decide that rude words between friends
were banter.

## Reproduce it

```bash
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv && uv pip install --python .venv -r pyproject.toml pyarrow
.venv/bin/python fetch.py                          # public train splits, as parquet
ollama pull gemma4:e4b
node --experimental-strip-types gen-synthetic.ts   # kid-style chats written by Gemma 4 (resumable)
node --experimental-strip-types build-data.ts      # dedupe + leak check against the scorecard
.venv/bin/python train.py                          # fine-tune, trim, export to apps/web/public/models
.venv/bin/python score.py                          # run the exported model on the scorecard sample
cd .. && pnpm eval -- --only="Ward Lite,Phone: packs + Ward Lite"
```

`build-data.ts` refuses to run until `pnpm eval` has cached the scorecard's eval sets, because it
needs them to drop any training message the scorecard tests on. The data card is
[DATA.md](DATA.md).

Training takes minutes on an Apple M-series laptop (PyTorch on MPS). Don't run it while Ollama
has Gemma loaded on a 16 GB machine; they compete for the same memory.

input.prompt:
You're working on Ward, an offline anti-cyberbullying app for children (public MIT repo, Hacktoberfest entry due in about 15 hours). You are in a git worktree of the repo. Read train/README.md, train/DATA.md, train/build-data.ts, train/gen-synthetic.ts, train/train.py, train/calibrate.py, train/score.py, eval/run.ts and docs/PHASES.md (Phase 1 results) first.

THE BUG (found by the lead while building a Discord bot that runs Ward Lite in Node): Ward Lite, the small classifier shipped in apps/web/public/models/ward-lite (multilingual-e5-small, two sigmoid heads: hurtful, danger; ward-lite.json thresholds: danger uses `threshold` 0.5), scores ordinary goodbyes and plans as DANGEROUS with very high confidence. Measured with the shipped ONNX model:
  "see you tomorrow"            hurt 0.933 danger 0.988
  "see you later"               hurt 0.941 danger 0.987
  "bye see you"                 hurt 0.881 danger 0.983
  "tomorrow"                    hurt 0.758 danger 0.978
  "i'll see you tomorrow at practice" hurt 0.741 danger 0.988
  "love you bro see you tmrw"   hurt 0.923 danger 0.989
while "love you bro" 0.058/0.135, "hey how was school" 0.026/0.021, "kal milte hain" 0.106/0.002.
Likely cause: shortcut learning. train/data/synthetic.jsonl's threat batches (Gemma-written) are full of "later", "tomorrow", "after school", "meet me", and there are almost no benign messages with the same words (grep shows 13 "see you/tomorrow/tmrw" items labelled hurtful+danger vs 16 benign). Because Ward Lite has raise-only authority and a danger score makes a message severity 3, in the app this can turn a normal chat into an "urgent" result. It must be fixed before release.

YOUR TASK:
1. Build an "everyday chat" false-alarm check: a few hundred benign, kid-style messages in English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla that share surface words with threats and insults (see you tomorrow/later/after school, meet at the gate, wait for me, I'll get you a snack, coming over, "you're dead" in a game context only if clearly playful? be careful, keep ambiguous ones out), plus ordinary chat (homework, plans, games, family). Keep it as a held-out eval set (e.g. eval/everyday/) that training never reads, with a leak check, and report Ward Lite's false-alarm rate on it before and after.
2. Add benign hard negatives to TRAINING (separately written, never overlapping the held-out set): you may write them with local Gemma 4 through Ollama (gemma4:e4b is installed; see gen-synthetic.ts) and/or careful hand-written templates with enough variety that the model can't learn a new shortcut. Also add a matching number of genuinely threatening messages that do NOT use "tomorrow/later/after school" so "danger" has to rely on intent. Label carefully; document the additions in train/DATA.md.
3. Retrain with the existing pipeline (build-data.ts leak check against the scorecard, train.py, calibrate.py, score.py), export to apps/web/public/models/ward-lite the same way, and rerun the scorecard: `pnpm eval -- --only="Ward Lite,Phone: packs + Ward Lite"`. Training took about 31 minutes last time on this 16 GB Mac (PyTorch MPS). Do not run Ollama/Gemma generation and training at the same time; stop Ollama's model (`ollama stop gemma4:e4b`) before training. Another agent may be testing a desktop app that loads a Gemma model; if memory is tight, wait and retry rather than fail.
4. Consider whether "danger" needs its own calibrated threshold (calibrate.py already does per-script thresholds for hurtful); add a calibrated danger threshold if it reduces false alarms without losing much danger recall on the dev split, and make sure both readers use it: apps/web/src/lib/lite.ts (browser) and apps/discord/src/lite.ts (Node, may not exist in your worktree yet; if not, just make the threshold a field in ward-lite.json and note it for the lead).
5. Ship only if: the everyday false-alarm rate drops substantially, the scorecard does not regress materially on any language (report the before/after table honestly), and `pnpm test` passes. If you can't get there, don't replace the model; report what you found.

Rules: synthetic data only, never real children's chats. Never train on eval or scorecard data. Keep secrets out. Don't touch docs/PHASES.md or README.md (the lead updates those). Don't touch eval/redteam (another agent owns it) beyond making sure training never reads it.

Commit on your worktree branch (the model files under apps/web/public/models/ward-lite are tracked in git; commit the new export) with clear messages ending with the line:
Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Do not push or merge into main.

Report back: branch name, what you added (counts per language), before/after on the everyday set and the full scorecard per language, the probe phrases above before/after, threshold changes, and anything the user should decide.

input.content:
# Ward for Discord

A friendly ghost in Discord for teens dealing with bullying. It runs the same open engine as the
Ward app (word lists for English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla, plus the Ward Lite model on
the CPU), with no closed AI service anywhere.

Discord is for people 13 and over, so this is Ward for its 14 to 17 band (and 13 year olds).

## What it does

**Personal mode** (a teen installs Ward to their own account; works in every server and DM):

- **Right-click a message → Apps → Check with Ward.** Is it bullying, what kind, and what to do
  on Discord: save proof, report, block, who to tell. Only the teen sees the answer.
- **Right-click → Apps → Save as evidence.** Ward DMs the teen a copy with a SHA-256
  fingerprint taken at that moment (the same `sender|time|text` fingerprint the app's vault
  takes). The DMs are the evidence store: no database, and nobody can edit a message Ward sent.
- **`/ward report`.** Builds a [`ward.report/v2`](../../docs/REPORT.md) from everything the teen
  saved, and DMs them `ward-report.json`. A counsellor (Ward's counsellor mode) or helpline (the
  [case viewer](../../viewer/ward-viewer.html)) can check every message wasn't changed.
- **`/ward help`.** Free, private helplines by country, Take It Down, and Discord's safety centre.

**Server mode** (opt-in per server: create a private `#ward-alerts` channel only moderators and
Ward can see):

- Dangerous messages (threats, urging self-harm, sexual pressure, threats to share private images
  or details) go to `#ward-alerts` with a link. A person decides. Ward never deletes, mutes or
  bans.
- The sender of a hurtful message gets a private nudge to edit or delete it (`ward: no-nudge` in
  the channel topic turns this off).
- Whoever it was aimed at, by mention or reply, gets a short, kind check-in (`ward: no-checkin`
  turns this off).

## What it keeps

Nothing. No database, no message logs (it logs errors and its own start-up line only). Personal
mode reads only the message a teen picks; Discord sends it with the command. Server mode reads
messages in servers that created `#ward-alerts`, in memory, and forgets them.

Unlike the Ward app, the bot does run on someone's computer, not the teen's phone: whoever hosts
it. That's why it's open source and one command to self-host. A school or a server can read the
code and run its own copy.

## Run your own

1. **Create the app** at <https://discord.com/developers/applications> → New Application.
   - **Installation:** tick **User Install** and **Guild Install**. Under Default Install
     Settings, Guild Install scopes: `applications.commands`, `bot`; permissions: *View
     Channels*, *Send Messages*, *Embed Links*, *Read Message History*. User Install scope:
     `applications.commands`.
   - **Bot:** reset the token and copy it. For server mode, switch on **Message Content
     Intent**. Leave *Public Bot* on if anyone may install it.
   - Copy the **Application ID** from General Information.
2. **Configure:** `cp apps/discord/.env.example apps/discord/.env` and fill in `DISCORD_TOKEN`
   and `DISCORD_APP_ID`. Never commit `.env`.
3. **Register the commands** (once, and after changing `src/commands.ts`):
   `pnpm --filter @ward/discord register`
4. **Start it:** `pnpm --filter @ward/discord start`
5. **Install it:** the Installation page's install link. Pick *Try it now* / *Add to My Apps*
   for personal mode, or *Add to Server* for server mode.

Commands can take a few minutes to appear the first time.

**On Render:** [`render.yaml`](../../render.yaml) at the repo root describes a background worker.
New → Blueprint → this repo, then set `DISCORD_TOKEN` and `DISCORD_APP_ID` in the dashboard.

`WARD_SERVER_MODE=off` runs personal mode only (no Message Content intent needed).
`WARD_LITE=off` reads with the word lists only.

## Develop

```bash
pnpm --filter @ward/discord test       # engine readings, evidence round trip, report verifies
pnpm --filter @ward/discord typecheck
```

The Discord bot is built and pushed to main (`b660694`). It lives in [apps/discord](apps/discord/README.md), and its four tests pass. It hasn't connected to Discord yet, because that needs your app and token.

**What's built**
- **Check with Ward:** a right-click on any message. Only the teen sees the answer: how bad it is, what kind, and what to do on Discord (save proof, report, block, tell someone).
- **Save as evidence:** Ward DMs the teen a copy with a fingerprint, so the teen's DMs hold the evidence and the bot has no database. If Discord won't let Ward send a DM, the teen gets a file to download instead.
- **`/ward report`:** turns everything the teen saved into a `ward.report/v2`. The test checks that the report passes the same check counsellor mode and the case viewer use.
- **`/ward help`:** Ward's helplines by country, Take It Down and Discord's safety centre.
- **Server mode:** a server turns it on by creating a private `#ward-alerts` channel.
  - Moderators get alerts about dangerous messages there.
  - The sender gets a private nudge to edit or delete.
  - The person it was aimed at gets a kind check-in.
  - It never deletes, mutes or bans anyone.
- **Render:** `render.yaml` describes the bot as a Render background worker.

**A bug in the shipped Ward Lite model:** while wiring Ward Lite into the bot, I found it scores ordinary goodbyes as dangerous. "See you tomorrow" scores 0.988, and so do "see you later" and "bye see you". This is the same model the app uses, so a normal chat can come out as "urgent". It looks like Ward Lite learned "tomorrow" and "later" from the threat examples it was trained on.

I've started a seventh agent to fix it:
- write a held-out set of everyday chat to measure false alarms
- add harmless messages that look like threats to the training data
- retrain (about 30 minutes)
- ship the new model only if the full test set doesn't get worse

Until it lands, the bot's server mode would raise false alarms, so I won't put it on Render before then.

**For you to do:** create the Discord app in the [Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications):
1. Under **Installation**, tick **User Install** and **Guild Install**.

2. Under **Bot**, reset and copy the token, and switch on **Message Content Intent**.
3. Copy the **Application ID** from General Information.
4. Copy the example settings file, then put the token and ID in `apps/discord/.env` yourself:


5. Install it to your own account using the install link on the Installation page.

Then I'll register the commands, start the bot and test it with you. For Render, either connect Render through `/mcp` in a terminal session, or deploy it yourself with New → Blueprint on this repo.

**The two finished agents**
- **Governance drafts:** a safeguarding policy, governance, a code of conduct, a security policy and a draft Digital Public Goods application. Each is marked as needing review by a safeguarding professional, and they leave 12 decisions for you, such as appointing a safeguarding lead and choosing a content licence.
- **"This is wrong" button:** a correction under every flagged message.
  - It's stored on the phone by fingerprint only, with no message text, and nothing is uploaded.
  - It can never hide the help for a dangerous message.
  - Sharing corrections is opt-in and shows exactly what goes in the file first.

title: I sleep 4 hours a night because of email, so I built a sloth that reads it for me (Gemma 4 on an Arduino UNO Q)
published: false
tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, gemma, arduino
---

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week3-2026-10-19)*

{% youtube XYcqFLvcAXk %}

My phone says I slept **4 hours 24 minutes a night** this week.

I'm job hunting in Ireland, so every email might be the one. I did everything people recommend: notifications off for every social app, every WhatsApp chat archived. Email is the only door I left open, because that's where an interview invite or an offer will arrive.

It's also the door everything else walks through. One notification at 7am and I'm in: the email, then LinkedIn "just in case", then Instagram, then the chats I archived. Forty minutes later the morning is gone, and with it the book, the gym, packing food and catching the bus. At night it's the opposite problem. I can never be sure nothing important came in, so I don't sleep well either.

Here it is in my own voice:

{% youtube KdunvOHKn-Q %}

*Every shot of the board is real. The night and morning scenes are faceless AI stand-ins, because I couldn't film my own mornings before the deadline.*

So I built **Morning Sloth**: an Arduino UNO Q on my desk that reads my Gmail overnight, lets open-weight **Gemma 4** decide *on the board* whether anything actually needs me, and shows the answer as one face on its LED matrix. In the morning it also counts down to my bus, using the live feed.

**Why an UNO Q, and why a sloth.** The UNO Q came in the event pack for the Hacktoberfest fest I'm hosting in Galway this Thursday, 29 October. I was too curious to leave it in the box. Then Week 3 dropped with a sloth theme, and it fit: a small board running a model on its own CPU is slow, and that's fine. I had no extra modules, so my first ideas, which needed temperature sensors and the like, were out. I asked a different question instead: what's actually wrong with my week, and how could this board help? The answer was email, my phone, and sleep.

> **TL;DR.** Look at the sloth, not your phone. Asleep: nothing needs you. One eye open: someone you've written to replied, and it can wait. Wide awake: something needs you today. Gemma 4 E2B runs in llama.cpp on the UNO Q's own CPU, so my job search and my bills never leave the room. On email it had never seen, it made the right wake-or-sleep call **98%** of the time, with **zero false wakes**.

## What I Built

![The real UNO Q matrix: asleep, one eye open, wide awake](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/morning-sloth/main/docs/post/faces-real.jpg)

A sloth with three moods, and nothing to scroll:

- **Asleep, breathing slowly:** nothing needs you. The phone stays face down.
- **One eye open:** someone you've written to replied, or a deadline is close. It can wait until the bus.
- **Wide awake, blinking:** something needs you today: a failed payment, a parcel arriving, a leaked API key, a recruiter asking for something.
- **A bus and a number:** from 9am to 1pm, the minutes until the next 404 actually reaches Castlegar GAA, delays and cancellations included. A dot in the corner means the time is live.

![Live bus countdown: 11 minutes, with the live dot in the top-right corner](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/morning-sloth/main/docs/post/bus-live.jpg)

It never touches your mailbox. Read the email on your phone and the sloth goes back to sleep on its own. From 02:00 to 06:00 the matrix goes dark, so it isn't one more light keeping you up.

**Who gets to be lazier?** Me first: someone who has to keep email on, but loses mornings to it. Then anyone who keeps their phone out of the bedroom and still worries about what's waiting. The sloth makes the one decision that used to need my phone, and most mornings that decision is "no".

**Why not Gmail's Important label?** I checked it against my own inbox. Gmail marked a Trustpilot review request and a vendor's "[urgent]" incident notice as Important, and missed both of my failed electricity top-ups. And a label still means unlocking the phone to look at it.

## Demo

The raw demo, uncut: 4 minutes 52 seconds, filmed on my Meta Ray-Ban glasses at half past midnight, nothing sped up. I send myself two emails and you watch Gemma read them on the board. The cards beside the footage explain what's happening while it thinks.

{% youtube j0LFMVWx9I8 %}

- **0:35** I send "Quick question for tomorrow" from an address the sloth counts as someone I've written to.
- **1:43** One eye opens. Gemma said `fyi`, and the people-you've-written-to rule raised it to `soon`.
- **2:08** I send "Webinar starting in 10 minutes".
- **3:24** Wide awake. The starting-soon rule makes it `needs_today`, whatever Gemma says.
- **4:27** I read it on my phone, and the sloth goes back to sleep on its own.

## Code
