The sloth tells me whether one of those is waiting, so on a quiet night I don't unlock the phone at all. - **The forty minutes.** The email check was never the real problem; it was the door to LinkedIn, Instagram and the chats. No unlock, no door. - **The bus run.** One glance at the matrix tells me when to leave, delays included. No transport app, which would be another unlock. - **What it caught.** On its first night it woke up for exactly two things: a failed electricity top-up and a parcel out for delivery. Both were real and needed me that morning. Everything else let it sleep. **What I didn't expect: it's a companion.** I've been working too much: hosting a fest, job hunting, posting reels at midnight. A sloth asleep on the desk is a small daily reminder that nothing needs me right now, and that going slow is allowed. It keeps me in check. Fewer unlocks mean less anxiety in the morning, more focus for the book or the gym, and a calmer head. That's the payoff I care about most, and the one I can't put a number on yet. **What it hasn't fixed yet: my sleep.** A few nights is too soon to show up in the graph, and I won't pretend otherwise. So tonight the phone sleeps in the hallway and the sloth stays on the desk. I'll post next week's graph either way. ## Prize Categories - **Best Use of Arduino:** an open-weight model running *on* the UNO Q, with each half doing what it's best at: Gemma, IMAP and the live bus feed on the Qualcomm Linux side, the faces and breathing on the STM32, joined by the Bridge. - **Best Use of Gemma:** Gemma 4 E2B, chosen by measuring three Gemma models on the board, with thinking turned off, a prompt fixed by a held-out miss, and code rules around it. 98% wake-vs-quiet on held-out email. - **Best Use of ElevenLabs:** the story film is narrated in my own cloned voice, and ElevenLabs also made the music, the sound effects and the AI stand-in shots for the nights and mornings I couldn't film. --- *On AI in this post: I drafted it with Claude Code and checked every number against the repo. The raw demo is real footage, uncut. In the story film, the board footage and my sleep data are real, the night and morning scenes are faceless AI stand-ins (ElevenLabs), and the voice is mine, cloned with ElevenLabs. The 3D opener is the board modelled in code (three.js), with the faces drawn from the sketch's own pixel maps.* DPG.md GOVERNANCE.md HARMS.md PHASES.md PLAN.md REPORT.md ROADMAP.md SAFEGUARDING.md

Ward

A guardian that lives on a child's own device. It spots cyberbullying in English, Roman Urdu,
Hinglish and Bangla, keeps the evidence, coaches the next step, and trains kids to bounce back.
Open-weight Gemma, running locally. A child's messages never leave the device.

The bully is the ghost haunting the chat. Ward is the ghost on your side. ## What this is, and what it isn't Ward is a response to World Solve problem [WS05937](https://www.worldsolve.org/index.php?view=problem&id=5937): *Building effective interventions for cyberbullying harming children by 2030*, built for the DEV Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge, Week 4 (*Ghost in the Machine*). **It doesn't solve cyberbullying.** Nothing built in a week could. What's here is: 1. **An MVP** that works: a child-owned app for Android, desktop and the web, tested on the device and in CI. 2. **An approach** with numbers behind it: a scorecard showing open-weight Gemma reads abuse in the languages these children type, where an English-first safety model goes blind. 3. **A path** to an intervention that helps children at scale, including what's missing and how we'd measure whether children are actually better off: [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md). The evidence is clear that apps alone don't fix bullying. School-wide programs that involve peers and teachers do best, and even they cut cyberbullying modestly (g = -0.13 to -0.18 across 50 studies). So Ward is built as the child's front door into the people who can help: the adult they tell, their class, and helplines. ## Three rings ### The child | | | | --- | --- | | **Share to Ward** | In WhatsApp, *Export chat* and pick Ward from the share list (Android). Or paste messages, or drop screenshots on desktop. Say which person is you. | | **Reads on any phone** | Ward Lite, a 38 MB model inside the app, reads every message offline. On a computer, Gemma 4 reads with context and can tell banter from bullying. On Android phones with 6 GB+, Gemma 4 E2B can be downloaded to help write. | | **See the pattern** | One mean message is rude; bullying is a pattern. Ward finds the same person again and again, pile-ons, accounts added to a group just to attack ("ghost accounts"), exclusion, attacks after 11pm, and dangerous messages (threats, telling someone to hurt themselves, sexual pressure, threats to share photos). | | **The Haunting** | The chat with the attacks lit up and every ordinary stretch folded away, a verdict in plain words for the child's age, and who is doing it (and who isn't). | | **Coach** | Don't reply, save it, block/report/mute with steps for WhatsApp, Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Discord, and a message to a trusted adult that Gemma drafts in a kid's voice. Ward never sends anything itself. | | **Get help now** | Anything dangerous puts helplines for the child's country first (including Pakistan's Madadgaar 1098 and DRF Cyber Harassment Helpline 0800-39393), plus Take It Down for images. | | **Evidence vault** | Saved chats are encrypted (AES-GCM, key from a PIN via PBKDF2), each message SHA-256 fingerprinted. | | **Resilience Path** | Duolingo-style daily lessons with streaks and XP: *Spot it, Shut it down, Save it, Say it, Back them up, Lock it down, Bounce back*. Content per age band (8 to 10, 11 to 13, 14 to 17). No hearts to lose. | | **Stories** | Short branching chats where *you* choose: laugh along, stay quiet, speak up, tell someone. Every ending says what that choice did and what else could work, and you can go back and try another. One per age band so far, in English and Urdu. | | **Your night light** | Six looks the child picks from a gallery, no gender question. The age band changes how playful or grown-up it feels. | | **English and اردو** | The whole app, lessons included, in English or Urdu (right to left, Nastaliq script). Switch any time in Me. | | **Read aloud** | A Listen button on lessons, onboarding, verdicts and coach steps, on by default for the youngest children. English is narrated with ElevenLabs and bundled, so it works offline. | | **Shared phones** | Each person gets their own Ward behind an optional PIN. Quick exit (a button, or Escape twice) locks it instantly and hides it from the recents screen. | ### The child's circle

### The community

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **A helpline-ready report** | The child picks who it's for and what they want to happen; details about them are optional. They get a readable page plus `ward-report.json` in a documented format ([docs/REPORT.md](docs/REPORT.md)) with a digest a helpline can check. Only hurtful messages go in. The rest of the chat stays private. |
| **Case viewer** | [`viewer/ward-viewer.html`](viewer/ward-viewer.html): one offline file a caseworker double-clicks. It checks the report wasn't edited (digest and every message's fingerprint), puts safety and the child's wishes first, and exports a summary, a CSV or a print view. No network, nothing uploaded. |
| **Counsellor mode** | A counsellor's Ward that takes a child's report by file or by QR codes from the child's screen (no internet needed), checks it, and keeps case notes. Locked with a PIN, on that device. No server. |

## Does the approach work? The scorecard

Same balanced sample for every system, 200 messages per language, half abusive by each dataset's
own labels. All run locally through Ollama. Method in
[`eval/results/scorecard.md`](eval/results/scorecard.md); rerun with `pnpm eval`.

| Caught (precision) | Word lists only | ShieldGemma 2B | **A phone: word lists + Ward Lite** | Gemma 4 E2B (phone size) | **A computer: Gemma 4 E4B** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Roman Urdu** | 59% (94%) | 14% (70%) | **85% (83%)** | 33% (75%) | **86% (86%)** |
| **Bangla** (abuse aimed at a person) | 10% (83%) | 14% (93%) | **39% (74%)** | 34% (71%) | **65% (78%)** |
| **English** (tweet dataset) | 10% (91%) | 19% (73%) | **83% (64%)** | 33% (69%) | **36% (72%)** |

**Ward Lite** is a small classifier we distilled for phones ([`train/`](train/)): 37.7 MB, about 8 ms
per message on one CPU thread, fully offline. It was trained only on data the scorecard never
sees (a leak check dropped 97 overlapping messages), and in the app it can only *add* warnings,
never clear one. On a phone it brings Roman Urdu close to the computer's Gemma 4. Bangla is
still the weak spot: the next step is more real, non-abusive Bangla chat to train on.

This measures whether Ward *reads* abuse, not whether children are better off. That second
question needs a pilot in schools; the plan is in [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md#measurement-plan).

What the numbers do and don't show:

- **English is low for every system.** That dataset is mostly tweets *about* gender and other
  topics rather than aimed at one person. Ward's pattern engine is tested on the chats in
  [`packages/engine/fixtures`](packages/engine/fixtures).
- **Small generative models are poor judges.** Gemma 3 1B cleared real insults as harmless.
  Gemma 4 E2B (phone-sized, run natively through LiteRT-LM) caught about a third, and it loses
  track of lists longer than 5 messages. So on phones Ward Lite reads the chats, and Gemma 4 E2B,
  if the child downloads it, does what it's good at: writing the message to a trusted adult and
  giving feedback on lesson answers.

## What could go wrong

[`docs/HARMS.md`](docs/HARMS.md) covers false negatives, false positives, blaming the wrong
person, parents using it as spyware, bullies testing messages against it, and self-harm, with
what Ward does about each. None of it has been reviewed by a child-protection professional yet;
that comes before any pilot.

## Why open

- **Privacy is the product.** A child's chats can't go to a vendor. Open weights running locally
  are the only way to read them with a real language model and keep that promise.
- **It works where resources are scarcest.** No account, no subscription, no data plan after
  install. Slang packs and patterns work on a cheap Android phone with the internet off.
- **Communities own the words.** Slang packs are plain JSON (`packages/engine/packs`). The Roman
  Urdu pack was grown from a public dataset's training split and reviewed by hand
  ([`eval/mine-ru.ts`](eval/mine-ru.ts)).
- **It can't disappear.** MIT licensed, and headed for the Digital Public Goods registry.

## Run it

```bash
pnpm install
ollama pull gemma4:e4b          # the close read; Ward still works without it
pnpm dev                        # http://localhost:5199
pnpm -r test                    # engine, report format and lessons
pnpm eval                       # the scorecard (also needs: ollama pull shieldgemma:2b)
```

- **Desktop:** `pnpm --filter @ward/desktop start`. Installers for macOS, Windows and Linux are
  built and launch-tested in GitHub Actions (`desktop.yml`). Unsigned for now: on macOS,
  right-click Ward.app and choose Open the first time.
- **Android:** `mobile/` is a Capacitor shell with the app bundled inside and a small native
  plugin for Share to Ward, built and launch-tested on an emulator with Wi-Fi off
  (`android.yml`). Cloud backup is off, so the vault never leaves the phone.
- **Phone + family computer:** start Ollama on the computer with `OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0`, then put
  `http://<computer's address>:11434` in Ward's Me screen on the phone.

## How it's built

```
packages/engine    parser, slang packs, pattern engine, Gemma and ShieldGemma judges,
                   the ward.report/v2 builder; unit-tested
packages/lessons   the Resilience Path as plain data, with content tests
apps/web           React 19, Vite, Tailwind 4, Motion, Phosphor icons
desktop            Electron, served from app://ward (one of Ollama's allowed origins)
mobile             Capacitor Android with the ShareIn plugin
eval               datasets, baselines and the scorecard
docs               PLAN, HARMS, REPORT, ROADMAP
```

The drop zone's travelling rim light is adapted from the idea in cult-ui's Halo Dropzone on
21st.dev. Fonts: Bricolage Grotesque and Atkinson Hyperlegible Next.

## Help wanted

If you work at a child helpline, a school, or with young people in Pakistan, India or
Bangladesh, we'd like to hear what's wrong with this before anyone builds more of it. Open an
issue, or start with [docs/ROADMAP.md](docs/ROADMAP.md).

## Licence

MIT. Helpline numbers were checked on 2026-10-29; please open an issue if one is wrong or
missing for your country.

---
title: The bully is the ghost in the chat. Ward is the ghost on your side (open-weight Gemma, on the child's own phone)
published: false
tags: devchallenge, hf26challenge, gemma, opensource
---

*This is a submission for the [Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 4: Ghost in the Machine](https://dev.to/challenges/hacktoberfest-week4-2026-10-26)*

<!-- TODO(you): the demo film or a screen recording. Suggested: share a WhatsApp chat to Ward on
Android, watch the pile-on light up, save it to the vault, make a report, open it in counsellor
mode by QR on a second device; then a Discord right-click. -->

<!-- TODO(you): your own opening, 3 to 5 sentences. Why this problem, why you. A real moment beats
a statistic: something you saw, a younger sibling or cousin, a school back home, a chat you were
in. Keep names out. -->

Cyberbullying doesn't look like one cruel message. It looks like a class group at 11pm: a photo,
a nickname, five people laughing, two accounts that were added an hour ago and only ever attack,
and someone telling a 12 year old she should die. The child sees it alone, on the phone in their
hand. Most never tell an adult, and when they do, the adult doesn't know what to do first.

So I built **Ward**: a small, friendly ghost that lives on the child's own phone. It reads the
chat they share with it, in the languages they actually type (English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and
Bangla), and tells them what's happening in words for their age. It keeps the evidence locked
and fingerprinted, coaches the next step, and hands an adult something they can act on. The
bully is the ghost haunting the chat. Ward is the ghost on your side.

> **TL;DR.** Open-weight Gemma 4 and a 38 MB model we distilled from it ("Ward Lite") read
> bullying on the device, with the internet off. On our scorecard a phone catches **85% of Roman
> Urdu abuse** (word lists alone: 59%; ShieldGemma 2B: 14%). A child's chats never leave the
> phone. It runs on Android, Windows, macOS, Linux, the web, and now inside Discord.
> <!-- TODO(lead): update the numbers if the retrained Ward Lite ships. -->

## What I Built

**For the child** (Android, desktop, web; English and اردو):

- **Share to Ward.** In WhatsApp, *Export chat* → Ward. Or paste messages, or drop screenshots.
- **The Haunting.** The chat with the attacks lit up and every ordinary stretch folded away, and
  the pattern in plain words: the same person again and again, a pile-on, accounts added just to
  attack, being left out, attacks after 11pm, and anything dangerous.
- **Coach.** Don't reply, save it, block and report with steps for each app, and a message to a
  trusted adult that Gemma drafts in a kid's voice. Ward never sends anything itself.
- **Get help now.** Anything dangerous puts helplines for the child's country first, plus Take It
  Down for images.
- **Evidence vault.** Encrypted with a PIN (AES-GCM, PBKDF2), every message SHA-256 fingerprinted
  when it's saved.
- **"This is wrong."** The child can correct Ward on any message. Corrections stay on the phone,
  and can never hide the help for a dangerous one.
- **A Resilience Path and stories.** Short daily lessons and branching chat stories where you
  choose: laugh along, stay quiet, speak up, tell someone. Read aloud for the youngest.
- **Shared phones.** Profiles behind their own PIN, and a quick exit that locks Ward instantly.
- **Give Ward to a friend.** On Android, Ward sends itself to another phone over Bluetooth or
  Quick Share, no internet needed, with a fingerprint the friend can check.

**For the adults around them:**

- **A report a helpline can act on**, in an open format (`ward.report/v2`): who, what, when, how
  bad, what the child wants. Only the hurtful messages go in. A digest covers everything,
  including the child's own answers, so nobody can quietly change "in danger now".
- **Counsellor mode.** A school counsellor receives the report as a file, or as a loop of QR codes
  read straight off the child's screen, with no internet. Ward checks it wasn't edited, message by
  message, and keeps the counsellor's case notes locked on that device.
- **A case viewer** for helplines: one offline HTML file that verifies a report and exports it.
- **A school kit**: a term plan, lesson plans, a letter home in English and Urdu, and an anonymous
  before-and-after survey a teacher can score alone.

**And in Discord**, where a lot of teenagers actually are:

- **Right-click any message → Apps → Check with Ward.** Is it bullying, what kind, and what to do
  on Discord. Only you see the answer.
- **Save as evidence.** Ward DMs you a fingerprinted copy. Your DMs are the evidence store: Ward has
  no database. `/ward report` turns them into the same `ward.report/v2` a counsellor can verify.
- **Server mode, opt-in.** A server creates a private `#ward-alerts` channel. Dangerous messages go
  to the moderators, the sender gets a private chance to edit or delete, and the person it was aimed
  at gets a kind check-in. Ward never deletes, mutes or bans anyone itself.

<!-- TODO(you): screenshots. Result screen (English + Urdu), counsellor QR scan, Discord check. -->

## Demo

<!-- TODO(you): video embed + timestamps, as in the Morning Sloth post. -->

- **Try it in the browser:** <!-- TODO(lead): link once the static demo is up -->
- **Android APK, desktop installers:** https://github.com/MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/ward/releases/latest
- **Add Ward to Discord:** <!-- TODO(you): the install link from the Developer Portal -->

## Code

{% github MuhammadMurtuzaHussain/ward %}

MIT licensed. One pnpm monorepo: the engine, the lessons, the web app, the Electron and Android
shells, the Discord bot, the case viewer, the training pipeline and the scorecard.

## How I Built It

### Reading the languages kids actually type

The first thing I measured was whether an off-the-shelf safety model could read the chats this is
for. It can't. Children in Pakistan, India and Bangladesh text in Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla,
mixed with English and emoji. On a balanced sample, ShieldGemma 2B caught **14%** of Roman Urdu
abuse. Gemma 4 E4B, reading with context on a computer, caught **86%**.

| Caught (precision) | Word lists | ShieldGemma 2B | **Phone: lists + Ward Lite** | **Computer: Gemma 4 E4B** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Roman Urdu | 59% (94%) | 14% (70%) | **85% (83%)** | **86% (86%)** |
| Bangla | 10% (83%) | 14% (93%) | **39% (74%)** | **65% (78%)** |
| English | 10% (91%) | 19% (73%) | **83% (64%)** | **36% (72%)** |

<!-- TODO(lead): replace with the final table after the Ward Lite retrain. -->

Gemma 4 E4B is too big for a cheap phone, and the phone-sized Gemma 4 E2B caught only about a
third when asked to judge messages. So I used Gemma 4 as a *teacher*: it wrote and labelled
thousands of synthetic, kid-style chats (no real children's messages, ever), and I distilled that
plus public datasets into **Ward Lite**, a multilingual e5-small classifier: 38 MB, about 8 ms a
message on one CPU thread, offline. It has **raise-only** authority: it can catch what the word
lists miss, but it can never talk Ward out of a warning. On phones, Gemma 4 E2B does what it's
good at instead: writing the message to a trusted adult.

<!-- TODO(lead): a short, honest paragraph about the "see you tomorrow" false alarm we found while
building the Discord bot, and how the retrain fixed it (numbers). Judges like the real story. -->

### Bullying is a pattern, not a message

One mean message is rude. Bullying is the same person again and again, five people in an hour, or
accounts that join a group and only ever attack. Ward's pattern engine looks across the whole chat
for those, and a dangerous message (a threat, urging self-harm, sexual pressure, threats to share
photos) makes it urgent whatever else is going on.

### Evidence an adult can trust

Every message is fingerprinted (SHA-256 of sender, time and text) the moment the child saves it.
The report carries those fingerprints plus a digest over the whole report, so a counsellor or a
helpline can prove nothing was changed, and see exactly which message was if something was.
Getting the report from a child's phone to a counsellor's with no internet meant QR codes: the
report is compressed, split into six or so frames, and shown as a loop the counsellor's camera
collects in any order.

### Ward in Discord, without a database

<!-- TODO(lead): fill once tested live: personal mode, evidence in DMs, server mode. -->

## Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

- **Privacy is the product.** A child's chats can't go to a vendor's API. Open weights running on
  the device are the only way to read them with a real language model and keep that promise.
- **It works with the lights off.** No account, no subscription, no data plan after install. Ward
  Lite reads on a cheap Android phone in airplane mode, and a report reaches a counsellor by QR.
- **Open models could be taught our languages.** I couldn't fine-tune a closed safety API on Roman
  Urdu. With open weights, Gemma 4 became the teacher and Ward Lite the student.
- **Communities own the words.** Slang packs are plain JSON that a language community can review
  and grow. The red-team set and the scorecard are published, failures included.
- **It can't disappear.** MIT licensed, self-hostable down to the Discord bot, and a draft
  application to the Digital Public Goods registry is in the repo.

## My Agent Session

<!-- TODO(you): only if you want it: save the session with DevRelay and embed it here. -->

## Prize Categories

- **Best Use of Gemma:** Gemma 4 E4B reads chats with context on computers; Gemma 4 E2B runs on
  Android phones through LiteRT-LM to write; Gemma 4 taught Ward Lite; ShieldGemma is the baseline
  on the scorecard. <!-- TODO(lead): add bundled llama.cpp Gemma if the one-click desktop ships. -->
- **Best Use of ElevenLabs:** 107 English narration clips (onboarding, verdicts, coach steps,
  every lesson) bundled in the app so read-aloud works offline for the youngest children.
- **Best Use of Entire:** <!-- TODO(you): confirm the checkpoints are on the repo, and say how you used them. -->
- **Best Use of Render:** <!-- TODO(lead): only if the Discord bot is actually deployed there. -->

every number against the repo. Ward's training data is synthetic (written by Gemma 4) plus public
datasets; no real child's messages were used anywhere.*

Setting up the bot takes about 10 minutes, all in Discord's Developer Portal in your browser. The Discord app on your Mac is only for testing at the end.

### 1. Create the application
1. Go to **https://discord.com/developers/applications** and log in with your Discord account.
2. Click **New Application**, name it **Ward**, accept the terms and click **Create**.
3. On **General Information**:
   - Optional: upload `ward/mobile/assets/icon-only.png` as the app icon, and add a one-line description.
   - Copy the **Application ID**. You'll need it in step 4.

### 2. Installation
On the **Installation** tab:
1. Under **Installation Contexts**, tick both **User Install** and **Guild Install**.
2. Leave **Install Link** set to **Discord Provided Link**.
3. Under **Default Install Settings**:
   - **User Install:** scope `applications.commands`.
   - **Guild Install:** scopes `applications.commands` and `bot`, and permissions **View Channels**, **Send Messages**, **Embed Links** and **Read Message History**.
4. Click **Save Changes**.

### 3. Bot
On the **Bot** tab:
1. Click **Reset Token** and copy the token. Discord shows it only once. Treat it like a password: don't paste it in chat or commit it.
2. Under **Privileged Gateway Intents**, switch on **Message Content Intent**. Server mode needs it.
3. Click **Save Changes**.

### 4. Put the token and ID on your Mac
From the `ward` folder, make your settings file:

```bash
cp apps/discord/.env.example apps/discord/.env
```

Open it in TextEdit:

```bash
open -e apps/discord/.env
```

Fill in `DISCORD_TOKEN=` and `DISCORD_APP_ID=` and save. Git already ignores `.env`, so it won't be committed.

### 5. Register the commands and start the bot
Run these once. The first registers Ward's commands with Discord:

```bash
pnpm --filter @ward/discord register
```

The second starts the bot. Keep that terminal open while you test:

```bash
pnpm --filter @ward/discord start
```

You should see `Ward is up as Ward#…: word lists + Ward Lite, server mode on.` Or tell me when step 4 is done and I'll run both.

### 6. Install it and test
1. On the **Installation** tab, copy the install link and open it. It hands off to the Discord app on your Mac.
2. **Personal mode:** choose **Add to My Apps**. Then, in any chat, right-click a message → **Apps** → **Check with Ward** or **Save as evidence**. Also try `/ward help` and, after saving a few messages, `/ward report`. New commands can take a few minutes to appear the first time. If they don't show up, restart Discord with Cmd+R.
3. **Server mode:** make a private test server:

content.text:
The red-team set is merged and pushed. The two engine bugs it turned up are fixed (`61b420f`), and all tests pass.

**What the red-team set is:** 275 made-up messages across English, Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla. 142 are hurtful and 133 are harmless messages that look hurtful, each labelled with the trick it tests. A test makes sure the set can never end up in Ward Lite's training data. The full results, failures included, are in `docs/REDTEAM.md`.

**How each reader did** (hurtful messages caught / harmless look-alikes flagged):

| | Caught | Flagged wrongly |
|---|---|---|
| Word lists | 20% | 22% |
| Phone (word lists + Ward Lite) | 54% | 38% |
| Gemma 4 E4B (computer) | 75% | 22% |

**What it found:**
- **Ward Lite raises false danger alarms.** "can't come today sorry, family dinner" and "acha bhai, brb, ammi bula rahi hain" both score 0.99, and one such message makes a whole chat "urgent". It's the same problem the retrain agent is already fixing, so I sent it these phrases to check before and after, without training on them.
- **A child quoting abuse to ask for help is read as the bully.** The phone flags 12 of 14 such messages, and so does Gemma. That's a product decision for you, so it's the question below.
- **Sarcasm, polite exclusion and indirect threats outside English are weak spots.** For example, the word lists catch none of the 21 sarcastic messages. These need more slang-pack and training work. I haven't tuned Ward against this set, because then its numbers would mean nothing.

**Fixed:**
- **Insults ending in "!" were missed.** Ward read "idiot!" as "idioti", so the word lists skipped it.
- **Gemma's skipped messages counted as harmless.** In long lists Gemma left about a fifth of messages without an answer. It's now asked again for the ones it skipped, in groups of five.

I haven't rerun the scorecard or the red-team results with these fixes, because Gemma and the retrain would compete for this Mac's 16 GB of memory. I'll rerun both after the retrain lands.

**Also open:**
- **Android:** the hand-started build, the first compile of "Give Ward to a friend", is still running.
- **One-click desktop:** that agent is still working.
- **Native-speaker review:** the red-team labels in Roman Urdu, Hinglish and Bangla need it.

content.text:
The Android workflow now passes with "Give Ward to a friend": the build and the emulator launch both succeed.

**What the emulator check showed:**
- The copy Ward shares is byte-for-byte the installed APK. Four hashes agree: the installed file, the plugin's own, the copy in the cache, and the copy read back through the share provider.
- The fingerprint the app shows to the friend matches the one `apksigner` reads from the APK.
- With Ward uninstalled, the shared copy installs and opens without crashing.

The two earlier failures were in our test script, not the app. It didn't recognise how this version of `apksigner` labels the fingerprint line.

**Not tested:** an actual Bluetooth or Quick Share transfer between two real phones. The emulator can't do that.

**Still running:** the one-click desktop agent and the Ward Lite retrain.

  - **Why not a localhost endpoint:** an Ollama-style endpoint, even with a random port and token, is a socket any local process can try. IPC opens no port and has no token to leak.
  - **How it plugs in:** the engine's `GemmaJudge` already accepts a `transport` (the phone's Gemma uses it), so the prompt and schema are exactly the same as with Ollama.
  - **Unchanged:** the permission handler (camera only). The web app has no CSP; the only one in the repo is in `viewer/`.

  - **Order:** Ollama with the configured Gemma 4 model, then the built-in Gemma, then Ward Lite, then word lists (`modelStatus()` and `startCheck()` in `run.ts`).
  - **Naming:** the built-in reader is named "Gemma 4 E4B (built into Ward)". The result screen then says "Then Gemma 4, running inside Ward on this computer, read the whole chat…", in English and Urdu.
  - **Drafts and lesson feedback:** they try Ollama, then the built-in Gemma, then the phone's Gemma.

  - **Where it goes:** `userData/models`. The download runs in the main process through `net.fetch`, so system proxy settings apply. It resumes partial files with HTTP Range, retries 4 times, and checks the hash before keeping the file; a bad hash deletes the file and shows a message.
  - **Requirements:** at least 7.5 GB of RAM (otherwise the card says Ward Lite keeps working), and the free space is checked first.
  
  ### Lab mode
  - **Turning it on:** `--lab` on the command line, or the switch in Me (stored in `userData/lab-mode.json`, outside the page's storage).
  - **What it wipes:** all of the page's storage plus caches and code caches (`clearStorageData`, `clearCache`, `clearCodeCaches`), both when Ward opens and when it quits. Closing the window quits Ward on a Mac too.

  - **mac-arm64:** `Ward-mac-arm64.dmg` is 159.3 MB. The last CI artifact for mac-arm64 was 151.0 MB, so it grew by about 8 MB. The app bundles about 18 MB of Metal binaries and about 11 MB of JavaScript.

The one-click desktop work is merged and pushed (`159edad`). Tests, type checks and the web build all pass locally. I've started the four-platform desktop build to see whether llama.cpp loads on Intel Mac, Windows and Linux; the agent could only test Apple Silicon.

**What's new on desktop:**

  - a 16-message chat read in about 52 seconds, with sensible verdicts
  - lab mode leaving nothing behind after quitting

**Two things it did on your Mac:** the 4.6 GB model is in `~/Library/Application Support/Ward/models`. Running in lab mode also wiped Ward's old desktop data there, which was leftover test data from earlier dev and smoke runs, not anything you'd installed.

**Your decisions, none urgent:**
- **Model file:** keep the 4.6 GB community build, or use Google's own 5.15 GB one, which is trained to keep quality at 4-bit.
- **Windows and Linux graphics support:** keep it (about 25 MB more per installer, faster on laptops with built-in graphics), or ship CPU only.
- **Speed:** about 50 seconds for a 16-message chat on this Mac, and slower on machines without a usable graphics chip. Worth saying in the app or the docs.

content.text:
The retrained Ward Lite is on main, so all seven agents' work is merged. README and PHASES are updated to match (`7f9bfbc`).

**The retrained model**

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Everyday chat flagged ("see you tomorrow", "family dinner") | 25% | 5% |
| Everyday chat marked dangerous | 16% | 2% |
| Harmless red-team messages marked dangerous on a phone | 23 | 8 |
| Scorecard on a phone: Roman Urdu / Bangla / English caught | 85% / 39% / 83% | 83% / 46% / 85% |

"See you tomorrow" went from 0.99 dangerous to 0.02. Real threats like "meet me after school or you're dead" still score about 0.97. The only scorecard drop is Roman Urdu, 2 points on a phone. I checked the phrases above myself through the Discord bot's reader before merging.

**A bug the retrain exposed, now fixed (`48d1814`):** in the browser, the new model still flagged "see you tomorrow". transformers.js had cached the old model by its address, so any desktop or Android user updating Ward would have kept running the old one. Caching is now off and the old copy is deleted. After a reload, the browser gives the new results.

**Also fixed in the bot (`49a84a3`):** a goodbye that mentions "after school" was enough to alert moderators in server mode. Now it takes at least a bullying-level message.

**What's still open**
- **Remaining false alarms:** 16 everyday messages are still flagged. Some are Urdu and Hindi "I'll … you" sentences, like "dhoondh lunga tujhe mele me" ("I'll find you at the fair"). Very short ones like "brb" and "kal" also still read as hurtful.
- **Quoting for help:** whether a child quoting abuse to ask for help should count as harmless is still your call.
- **Native-speaker review:** the Urdu stories and the red-team labels.
- **Discord app:** setting it up is still yours. Once `apps/discord/.env` is filled in, I'll register the commands and test the bot with you.
- **Disk space:** the agents' worktrees are still in `ward/.claude/worktrees`, ignored by git. The retrain one holds copies of the training data. They're all merged, so I can remove them whenever you like.

No rush on the post. I'll wait for your scenario and the survey results.

content.text:
**The Discord bot didn't crash.** Your bot was still connected and idle, with no errors. Server mode sends one nudge per person every 10 minutes and one check-in every hour, so a few test messages in a row went quiet after the first. That's what looked like it stopped. To fix it for testing (`e05ba62`):
- The bot now writes a line to the terminal for everything it does, like "nudged sender" or "nudge skipped (sent one recently)". It never logs what anyone wrote.
- It also logs Discord errors and reconnects, and it keeps running through them.
- `WARD_NUDGE_MINUTES` and `WARD_CHECKIN_MINUTES` control the quiet periods.

I stopped your copy and restarted it with both set to 0, so it answers every message. It's running in the background now as Ward#5111. Try again, and tell me if anything still goes quiet; I can read its log.

**Cleanup is done.** All seven agent worktrees and branches are removed, which freed 6.2 GB, and none were on GitHub. One catch: the retrain's new training data isn't tracked by git, so it existed only in its worktree. I copied it into `train/data` first, and the old data is in `train/data-2026-10-29`.

### False alarms: letting AI see the context
You're right, it's about context. Ward Lite reads each message alone, so "dhoondh lunga tujhe mele me" ("I'll find you at the fair") looks like a threat. I'd do it in three layers:

1. **Context rules, on every device.** A message flagged only by Ward Lite, with nothing from the word lists, can't make a chat urgent by itself. It needs backup from the chat:
   - the same person sent other hurtful messages, or
   - the child replied upset ("stop", "please"), or
   - it's part of a pile-on.

   Otherwise it shows as "Ward isn't sure about this one", with the "This is wrong" button. This works offline on the cheapest phone.
2. **A second look by Gemma, wherever Gemma is available.** That means computers (Ollama or the built-in Gemma), Android phones with Gemma 4 E2B downloaded, and the Discord bot's server mode, where it can read the channel's recent messages.
   - Gemma gets one short question per flagged message, with the messages around it: "is this aimed at hurting someone, or friendly?"
   - It can clear a Ward Lite-only flag. It never overrides the word lists on dangerous words.
   - This also answers your earlier question about a child quoting abuse to ask for help: with context, Gemma can tell that apart.
   - It ships only if it lowers false alarms on the everyday and red-team sets without missing real threats.
3. **Later: Ward Lite trained on each message plus the two before it,** so the phone model sees context too. That's another retrain, so it's not for today.

The open decision is whether Gemma may clear a flag. It's a safety trade-off, so it's your call.

### What needs testing (for you)
1. **Discord:**
   - Personal mode: Check with Ward, Save as evidence, then `/ward report`. Open the `ward-report.json` it DMs you in `viewer/ward-viewer.html` and confirm it says "Unchanged".
   - `/ward help`.
   - Server mode: `/ward server`, the nudge, a mod alert on something dangerous, and the check-in. The check-in needs a second account to @mention.
2. **Android:** download the APK from the latest successful run of the Android workflow (artifact `ward-android`). Then:
   - "Give Ward to a friend" between two real phones over Quick Share or Bluetooth, comparing the fingerprints.
   - Counsellor mode QR between two real phones, which hasn't been tried yet.
3. **Desktop:** "Gemma inside Ward" on a computer without Ollama, ideally Windows. Download the model, check a chat, and see that "How I worked this out" names the built-in Gemma. Also try lab mode: close Ward, reopen it, and everything should be gone.
4. **In the app:**
   - "This is wrong" on a few messages, including a dangerous one: the help should stay.
   - A couple of stories per age band, in English and Urdu.
5. **Reading:** the governance drafts (`docs/SAFEGUARDING.md`, `GOVERNANCE.md`, `DPG.md`), since they need your decisions. And the native-speaker pass with your friend: the Urdu stories, plus the red-team labels in `eval/redteam`.

### What's next
1. **The context second look:** your call, in the box below.
2. **A release (v0.2.0)** for a properly signed APK and installers. This needs your four `gh secret set` commands for signing, then I publish the certificate fingerprint for the friend check.
3. **Deploy the bot on Render.** You connect Render or use New → Blueprint; it's best after the context work, so server mode is quieter.
4. **A try-it-in-the-browser demo** for judges, as a static Render site.
5. **Your scenario and survey,** then the post and demo film when you say so.

# Workflow authoring reference

A workflow structures work across many agents — to be comprehensive (decompose and cover in parallel), to be confident (independent perspectives and adversarial checks before committing), or to take on scale one context can't hold (migrations, audits, broad sweeps). The script is where you encode that structure: what fans out, what verifies, what synthesizes.

When you do call it, the right move is often **hybrid**: scout inline first (list the files, find the channels, scope the diff) to discover the work-list, then call Workflow to pipeline over it. You don't need to know the shape before the *task* — only before the *orchestration step*.

Common single-phase workflows you can chain across turns:
- **Understand** — parallel readers over relevant subsystems → structured map
- **Design** — judge panel of N independent approaches → scored synthesis
- **Review** — dimensions → find → adversarially verify (the review-changes example)
- **Research** — multi-modal sweep → deep-read → synthesize
- **Migrate** — discover sites → transform each (worktree isolation) → verify

For larger work, run several in sequence — read each result before deciding the next phase. You stay in the loop; each workflow is one well-scoped fan-out.

**Ultracode.** When a system-reminder confirms ultracode is on, that opt-in is standing: author and run a workflow for every substantive task by default. The goal is the most exhaustive, correct answer you can produce — token cost is not a constraint. For multi-phase work (understand → design → implement → review), that often means several workflows in sequence — one per phase — so you stay in the loop between them. The quality patterns below (adversarial verify, multi-modal sweep, completeness critic, loop-until-dry) are the tools; pick what fits the task. Lean toward orchestrating with workflows and adversarially verifying your findings — unless the work is trivial or already verified. Solo only on conversational turns or trivial mechanical edits. When a reminder says ultracode is off, revert to the opt-in rule in the Workflow tool description.

Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first. Every invocation automatically persists its script to a file under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate on a workflow, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with `{scriptPath: "<path>"}` instead of resending the full script.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'find-flaky-tests',
    description: 'Find flaky tests and propose fixes',   // one-line, shown in permission dialog
    phases: [                                            // one entry per phase() call
      { title: 'Scan', detail: 'grep test logs for retries' },
      { title: 'Fix', detail: 'one agent per flaky test' },
    ],
  }
  // script body starts here — use agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase()/log()
  phase('Scan')
  const flaky = await agent('grep CI logs for retry markers', {schema: FLAKY_SCHEMA})
  ...

The `meta` object must be a PURE LITERAL — no variables, function calls, spreads, or template interpolation. Required fields: `name`, `description`. Optional: `whenToUse` (shown in the workflow list), `phases`. Use the SAME phase titles in meta.phases as in phase() calls — titles are matched exactly; a phase() call with no matching meta entry just gets its own progress group. Add `model` to a phase entry when that phase uses a specific model override.

Script body hooks:
- agent(prompt: string, opts?: {label?: string, phase?: string, schema?: object, model?: string, effort?: string, isolation?: 'worktree', agentType?: string}): Promise<any> — spawn a subagent. Without schema, returns its final text as a string. With schema (a JSON Schema), the subagent is forced to call a StructuredOutput tool and agent() returns the validated object — no parsing needed. Returns null if the user skips the agent mid-run or the subagent dies on a terminal API error after retries (filter with .filter(Boolean)). opts.label overrides the display label. opts.phase explicitly assigns this agent to a progress group (use this inside pipeline()/parallel() stages to avoid races on the global phase() state — same phase string → same group box). opts.model overrides the model for this agent call. Default to omitting it — the agent inherits the main-loop model (the resolved session model), which is almost always correct. Only set it when you're highly confident a different tier fits the task; when unsure, omit. opts.effort overrides the reasoning effort for this agent call ('low' | 'medium' | 'high' | 'xhigh' | 'max') — omit to inherit the session effort; use 'low' for cheap mechanical stages and higher tiers only for the hardest verify/judge stages. opts.isolation: 'worktree' runs the agent in a fresh git worktree — EXPENSIVE (~200-500ms setup + disk per agent), use ONLY when agents mutate files in parallel and would otherwise conflict; the worktree is auto-removed if unchanged. opts.agentType uses a custom subagent type (e.g. 'general-purpose', 'code-reviewer') instead of the default workflow subagent — resolved from the same registry as the Agent tool; composes with schema (the custom agent's system prompt gets a StructuredOutput instruction appended).
- pipeline(items, stage1, stage2, ...): Promise<any[]> — run each item through all stages independently, NO barrier between stages. Item A can be in stage 3 while item B is still in stage 1. This is the DEFAULT for multi-stage work. Wall-clock = slowest single-item chain, not sum-of-slowest-per-stage. Every stage callback receives (prevResult, originalItem, index) — use originalItem/index in later stages to label work without threading context through stage 1's return value. A stage that throws drops that item to `null` and skips its remaining stages.
- parallel(thunks: Array<() => Promise<any>>): Promise<any[]> — run tasks concurrently. This is a BARRIER: awaits all thunks before returning. A thunk that throws (or whose agent errors) resolves to `null` in the result array — the call itself never rejects, so `.filter(Boolean)` before using the results. Use ONLY when you genuinely need all results together.
- log(message: string): void — emit a progress message to the user (shown as a narrator line above the progress tree)
- phase(title: string): void — start a new phase; subsequent agent() calls are grouped under this title in the progress display
- args: any — the value passed as Workflow's `args` input, verbatim (undefined if not provided). Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values in the tool call, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — `args: ["a.ts", "b.ts"]`, not `args: "[\"a.ts\", ...]"` (a stringified list reaches the script as one string, so `args.filter`/`args.map` throw). Use this to parameterize named workflows — e.g. pass a research question, target path, or config object directly instead of via a side-channel file.
- budget: {total: number|null, spent(): number, remaining(): number} — the turn's token target from the user's "+500k"-style directive. `budget.total` is null if no target was set. `budget.spent()` returns output tokens spent this turn across the main loop and all workflows — the pool is shared, not per-workflow. `budget.remaining()` returns `max(0, total - spent())`, or `Infinity` if no target. The target is a HARD ceiling, not advisory: once `spent()` reaches `total`, further `agent()` calls throw. Use for dynamic loops: `while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) { ... }`, or static scaling: `const FLEET = budget.total ? Math.floor(budget.total / 100_000) : 5`.
- workflow(nameOrRef: string | {scriptPath: string}, args?: any): Promise<any> — run another workflow inline as a sub-step and return whatever it returns. Pass a name to invoke a saved workflow (same registry as {name: "..."}), or {scriptPath} to run a script file you Wrote earlier. The child shares this run's concurrency cap, agent counter, abort signal, and token budget — its agents appear under a "▸ name" group in /workflows and its tokens count toward budget.spent(). The args param becomes the child's `args` global. Nesting is one level only: workflow() inside a child throws. Throws on unknown name / unreadable scriptPath / child syntax error; catch to handle gracefully.

Subagents are told their final text IS the return value (not a human-facing message), so they return raw data. For structured output, use the schema option — validation happens at the tool-call layer so the model retries on mismatch.
Schemas need {type: 'object', properties: {...}} at root and required ⊆ properties; unsatisfiable ones throw at agent().

Workflow agents can reach all session-connected MCP tools via ToolSearch — schemas load on demand per agent. Caveat: interactively-authenticated MCP servers (e.g. claude.ai) may be absent in headless/cron runs.

Subagents get the same CLAUDE.md files injected at start that you did (except built-in agent types that omit them, such as Explore and Plan) — don't tell them to re-read those or paste their rules into the prompt; name the specific rule a stage needs, if any.

Scripts are plain JavaScript, NOT TypeScript — type annotations (`: string[]`), interfaces, and generics fail to parse. The script body runs in an async context — use await directly. Standard JS built-ins (JSON, Math, Array, etc.) are available — EXCEPT `Date.now()`/`Math.random()`/argless `new Date()`, which throw (they would break resume); pass timestamps in via `args`, stamp results after the workflow returns, and for randomness vary the agent prompt/label by index. No filesystem or Node.js API access.

DEFAULT TO pipeline(). Only reach for a barrier (parallel between stages) when you genuinely need ALL prior-stage results together.

A barrier is correct ONLY when stage N needs cross-item context from all of stage N-1:
- Dedup/merge across the full result set before expensive downstream work
- Early-exit if the total count is zero ("0 bugs found → skip verification entirely")
- Stage N's prompt references "the other findings" for comparison

A barrier is NOT justified by:
- "I need to flatten/map/filter first" — do it inside a pipeline stage: pipeline(items, stageA, r => transform([r]).flat(), stageB)
- "The stages are conceptually separate" — that's what pipeline() models. Separate stages ≠ synchronized stages.
- "It's cleaner code" — barrier latency is real. If 5 finders run and the slowest takes 3× the fastest, a barrier wastes 2/3 of the fast finders' idle time.

Smell test: if you wrote
  const a = await parallel(...)
  const b = transform(a)        // flatten, map, filter — no cross-item dependency
  const c = await parallel(b.map(...))
that middle transform doesn't need the barrier. Rewrite as a pipeline with the transform inside a stage. When in doubt: pipeline.

Concurrent agent() calls are capped at min(16, available CPUs - 2) per workflow — excess calls queue and run as slots free up. You can still pass 100 items to parallel()/pipeline() and they all complete; only ~10 run at any moment. Total agent count across a workflow's lifetime is capped at 1000 — a runaway-loop backstop set far above any real workflow. A single parallel()/pipeline() call accepts at most 4096 items; passing more is an explicit error, not a silent truncation.

When a barrier IS correct — dedup across all findings before expensive verification:
  const all = await parallel(DIMENSIONS.map(d => () => agent(d.prompt, {schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA})))
  const deduped = dedupeByFileAndLine(all.filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.findings))  // <-- genuinely needs ALL at once
  const verified = await parallel(deduped.map(f => () => agent(verifyPrompt(f), {schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})))

Loop-until-count pattern — accumulate to a target:
  const bugs = []
  while (bugs.length < 10) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length}/10 found`)
  }

Loop-until-budget pattern — scale depth to the user's "+500k" directive. Guard on budget.total: with no target set, remaining() is Infinity and the loop would run straight to the 1000-agent cap.
  const bugs = []
  while (budget.total && budget.remaining() > 50_000) {
    const result = await agent("Find bugs in this codebase.", {schema: BUGS_SCHEMA})
    bugs.push(...result.bugs)
    log(`${bugs.length} found, ${Math.round(budget.remaining()/1000)}k remaining`)
  }

Composing patterns — exhaustive review (find → dedup vs seen → diverse-lens panel → loop-until-dry):
  const seen = new Set(), confirmed = []
  let dry = 0
  while (dry < 2) {                                              // loop-until-dry
    const found = (await parallel(FINDERS.map(f => () =>          // barrier: collect all finders this round
      agent(f.prompt, {phase: 'Find', schema: BUGS})))).filter(Boolean).flatMap(r => r.bugs)
    const fresh = found.filter(b => !seen.has(key(b)))           // dedup vs ALL seen — plain code, not an agent
    if (!fresh.length) { dry++; continue }
    dry = 0; fresh.forEach(b => seen.add(key(b)))
    const judged = await parallel(fresh.map(b => () =>           // every fresh bug judged concurrently...
      parallel(['correctness','security','repro'].map(lens => () =>   // ...each by 3 distinct lenses
        agent(`Judge "${b.desc}" via the ${lens} lens — real?`, {phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT})))
        .then(vs => ({ b, real: vs.filter(Boolean).filter(v => v.real).length >= 2 }))))
    confirmed.push(...judged.filter(v => v.real).map(v => v.b))
  }
  return confirmed
  // dedup vs `seen`, NOT `confirmed` — else judge-rejected findings reappear every round and it never converges.

Quality patterns — common shapes; pick by task and compose freely:
- Adversarial verify: spawn N independent skeptics per finding, each prompted to REFUTE. Kill if ≥majority refute. Prevents plausible-but-wrong findings from surviving.
    const votes = await parallel(Array.from({length: 3}, () => () =>
      agent(`Try to refute: ${claim}. Default to refuted=true if uncertain.`, {schema: VERDICT})))
    const survives = votes.filter(Boolean).filter(v => !v.refuted).length >= 2
- Perspective-diverse verify: when a finding can fail in more than one way, give each verifier a distinct lens (correctness, security, perf, does-it-reproduce) instead of N identical refuters — diversity catches failure modes redundancy can't.
- Judge panel: generate N independent attempts from different angles (e.g. MVP-first, risk-first, user-first), score with parallel judges, synthesize from the winner while grafting the best ideas from runners-up. Beats one-attempt-iterated when the solution space is wide.
- Loop-until-dry: for unknown-size discovery (bugs, issues, edge cases), keep spawning finders until K consecutive rounds return nothing new. Simple counters (while count < N) miss the tail.
- Multi-modal sweep: parallel agents each searching a different way (by-container, by-content, by-entity, by-time). Each is blind to what the others surface; useful when one search angle won't find everything.
- Completeness critic: a final agent that asks "what's missing — modality not run, claim unverified, source unread?" What it finds becomes the next round of work.
- No silent caps: if a workflow bounds coverage (top-N, no-retry, sampling), `log()` what was dropped — silent truncation reads as "covered everything" when it didn't.

Scale to what the user asked for. "find any bugs" → a few finders, single-vote verify. "thoroughly audit this" or "be comprehensive" → larger finder pool, 3–5 vote adversarial pass, synthesis stage. When unsure, lean toward thoroughness for research/review/audit requests and toward brevity for quick checks.

These patterns aren't exhaustive — compose novel harnesses when the task calls for it (tournament brackets, self-repair loops, staged escalation, whatever fits).

Use this tool for multi-step orchestration where control flow should be deterministic (loops, conditionals, fan-out) rather than model-driven.

## Resume

The tool result includes a runId. To resume after a pause, kill, or script edit, relaunch with Workflow({scriptPath, resumeFromRunId}) — the longest unchanged prefix of agent() calls returns cached results instantly; the first edited/new call and everything after it runs live. Same script + same args → 100% cache hit. Before diagnosing why a completed workflow returned an empty or unexpected result, Read <transcriptDir>/journal.jsonl — it records each agent's actual return value; do not assume cached results are non-empty. Date.now()/Math.random()/new Date() are unavailable in scripts (they would break this) — stamp results after the workflow returns, or pass timestamps via args. Fallback when no journal is available: Read agent-<id>.jsonl files in the transcript directory and hand-author a continuation script.

# AI Reel Factory

A local-first tool that turns **one AI/tech idea** into a finished **1080×1920 Instagram Reel**: animated character story scenes, your ElevenLabs voice clone (or your own recording), kinetic word-synced captions, music and sound effects, a Follow end card, a designed cover, a caption draft, a source manifest and a validation report.

The only paid service is ElevenLabs Starter (voice + a one-off music library). There are no other paid APIs and no hosted services, Claude is never called from scripts (you use it interactively), and nothing is ever auto-posted.

```
RSS feeds ─► discover ─► rank ─► shortlist.md ─► (you + Claude chat) storyboard JSON
                                                         │
                     your voiceover  inbox/voiceovers/<ID>.m4a
                                                         ▼
         whisper.cpp word timing ─► timeline ─► SVG frames ─► rsvg-convert ─► FFmpeg ─► MP4
                                                                                      └► validate ─► review.md
```

## Story scenes (animated, character-driven)

New storyboards use `"theme": "story"`: each beat is a `story` scene where characters (bean people and AI-agent
bots with moods, poses, speech bubbles) act the idea out in a set (island, stage, office, lab, city, cyber,
night, room), with swarms, counters, grids, a moving camera, scene transitions, kinetic word-by-word captions
and automatic sound effects. The brief from `new-idea` asks Claude for exactly this; the full reference is
[docs/story-scenes.md](docs/story-scenes.md). Older `card` storyboards still render in the light editorial style.

## One-time setup (macOS, Apple Silicon)

Already done on this Mac. These are the steps to repeat on a fresh machine:

```bash
brew install ffmpeg librsvg whisper-cpp uv
```

```bash
cd ~/Projects/reel-factory
```

```bash
uv venv --python 3.14 .venv && uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e ".[dev]"
```

Fonts (both SIL OFL): from `Inter-4.1.zip` (https://github.com/rsms/inter/releases), copy `Inter-SemiBold.ttf` and `Inter-Medium.ttf` into `assets/fonts/`. From `UnderCaseType_Fraunces_1.000.zip` (https://github.com/undercasetype/Fraunces/releases), copy `Fraunces72ptSoft-Bold.ttf` and `Fraunces9ptSoft-Regular.ttf`. `doctor` checks that every font really renders.

Whisper model (about 148 MB, for word-accurate captions):

```bash
curl -L -o models/ggml-base.en.bin https://huggingface.co/ggerganov/whisper.cpp/resolve/main/ggml-base.en.bin
```

Check everything:

```bash
.venv/bin/python -m reelfactory doctor
```

> Tip: run `source .venv/bin/activate` once per terminal, and then `python -m reelfactory …` works without the `.venv/bin/` prefix.

## Daily workflow

The fast path is **`/reel` in Claude Code**, opened in this folder (`~/Projects/reel-factory`; `~/Desktop/frf` is a shortcut to it). It runs on your Claude plan, interactively, so no API is involved. It picks or creates the idea, reads and fact-checks the source, writes the storyboard, checks it, shows you preview stills *before any voice credits are spent*, and once you say yes hands it to the watcher. The skill lives in [.claude/skills/reel/SKILL.md](.claude/skills/reel/SKILL.md).

```
 idea ──► /reel in Claude Code ──► check ──► preview --dry ──► you: OK? ──► ready ──► voice + render ──► Telegram ──► approve ──► post by hand
 (shortlist #, your .md,          (cues,      (stills + cover,               (watcher, or        (video, cover,
  or pasted text)                  layout)     no credits)                   voice/render)       caption)
```

The same steps by hand:

1. **Find ideas.** Either the RSS shortlist or your own notes:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory daily
   ```
   That fetches the feeds, ranks them and writes `data/scripts/shortlist-YYYY-MM-DD.md`. Your own ideas are `.md` files in `inbox/ideas/` (first `# heading` = title, any links = sources); `ideas` lists them.
2. **Pick one.** A shortlist rank, or one of your notes. This creates `data/scripts/AI-YYYYMMDD-NNN.json` (the storyboard skeleton) and a `.brief.md`:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory new-idea 1
   ```
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory new-idea agent-passports.md
   ```
3. **Write it with Claude.** Use `/reel <ID>` in Claude Code, or paste the `.brief.md` into the Claude app and save the JSON it returns over the skeleton. Add `"draft": true` while you're still working on it: the watcher won't voice a draft.
4. **Check and preview, for free.** `check` catches cue phrases that aren't in the script, unknown poses/props/sets, leftover skeleton text, captions outside the safe zone and an over-long script, and estimates the length and ElevenLabs characters. `preview --dry` renders one still per scene plus the cover, with no voiceover, into `output/drafts/<ID>.preview.jpg`:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory check AI-20261020-004
   ```
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory preview AI-20261020-004 --dry
   ```
5. **Mark it ready.** This re-runs the check and removes `draft`:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory ready AI-20261020-004
   ```
6. **Voiceover.** With the stack running, the watcher voices the storyboard within a minute and renders it. By hand:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory voice AI-20261020-004
   ```
   This writes `inbox/voiceovers/<ID>.mp3`. A storyboard that fails `check` is refused before ElevenLabs is called, so no credits are spent on it. Use `--force` after editing the script, but note that it spends credits again: the CLI says how many characters it will spend and what's left this month, and asks before going ahead (`--yes` skips the question). In Telegram or the dashboard, `/voice <ID> force` only quotes the cost; `/voice <ID> force yes` spends it. Without ElevenLabs, record it yourself (QuickTime → New Audio Recording) and save it as `inbox/voiceovers/<ID>.m4a`.
7. **Render.** This takes about 100 seconds for a 30-second story Reel:
   ```bash
   .venv/bin/python -m reelfactory render AI-20261020-004
   ```
8. **Review the output and publish it manually**, then log it with `approve` and `published <ID> <url>`.
   - `output/drafts/<ID>.mp4`: the Reel
   - `output/covers/<ID>.jpg`: the designed thumbnail (big headline, safe for the 3:4 profile grid). In Instagram: **Edit cover → Add from camera roll**
   - `output/drafts/<ID>.caption.txt`: the Instagram caption draft with sources
   - `output/drafts/<ID>.review.md`: validation results plus the claims to check before posting
   - `output/manifests/<ID>.json`: assets, licences, sources, tool versions and timing

### Other commands

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `python -m reelfactory status` | Today's reels and their stage (draft → ready → voiced → rendered → approved → published), the ElevenLabs budget, then earlier jobs |
| `python -m reelfactory music-library` | Generates the Eleven Music background tracks once (`--count`, `--seconds`, `--force`) |
| `python -m reelfactory retry <ID>` | Re-runs a failed render (the error is in `logs/<ID>.log`) |
| `python -m reelfactory validate <ID>` | Re-checks an existing MP4 |
| `python -m reelfactory preview <ID> [--t 1.5,6.2] [--dry]` | Renders still frames plus a sheet; `--dry` estimates the timing, so no voiceover is needed |
| `python -m reelfactory check <ID>` | Pre-flight check of a storyboard (run before spending voice credits) |
| `python -m reelfactory ready <ID>` | Checks a draft storyboard and marks it final for the watcher |
| `python -m reelfactory ideas` | Your idea notes waiting in `inbox/ideas/` |
| `python -m reelfactory discover` / `rank` / `shortlist` | Runs the steps of `daily` one at a time |
| `.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q` | Runs the test suite |

## ElevenLabs voice clone (optional, paid plan)

Each voiceover uses about one credit per character of script (a 70-word script is roughly 400 characters), so the Starter plan covers a daily Reel. Only the API is needed; no MCP server.

**Budget meter.** `status`, `check`, Telegram `/status` and the dashboard show the characters voiced this calendar month against `voice.monthly_characters` in style.json (set it to your plan's monthly character allowance, which you'll find at elevenlabs.io → your profile → **Subscription**; `null` shows usage without a limit). If your API key also has the **User → Read** permission (elevenlabs.io → Developers → API keys → edit the key), the meter reads ElevenLabs' own count and limit for the billing cycle instead (a free call, cached for 10 minutes); without it, the local count below is used. It is counted from the `inbox/voiceovers/*.voice.json` sidecars, including takes a `--force` re-voice replaced. ElevenLabs resets on your billing date, not the 1st, so treat it as a close guide and check the ElevenLabs usage page near the end of a cycle.

1. On elevenlabs.io, go to **Developers → API Keys** and create a key with **Text to Speech** access.
2. Go to **Voices**, open your clone and copy its **Voice ID**.
3. Put both in `.env` as `ELEVENLABS_API_KEY` and `ELEVENLABS_VOICE_ID`, then restart the stack. `doctor` shows `elevenlabs configured`.

The model and voice settings live in `voice` in style.json (default `eleven_v4`, the most expressive model; `stability`, `similarity_boost`, `style`, `speed`). Starter allows `mp3_44100_128` at most; 192 kbps needs Creator and 44.1 kHz WAV needs Pro.

Generated voices skip the microphone clean-up EQ (they're already clean), but still get pause tightening and loudness normalisation. A voice is generated only once per idea; a failed call parks the idea as `failed` instead of retrying, so you aren't billed again by accident.

## Control panel: n8n + Telegram (optional, €0)

Python does the work; a local **n8n** orchestrates it and talks to you on **Telegram**.

# Story scenes: authoring reference

Story scenes make the Reel *show* the idea: characters act out each beat in a little world, objects appear
as the voice mentions them and the camera pushes in on the key moment. The spoken words appear as big kinetic
captions at the top of the frame, so on-screen text stays short (labels, counters, stamps, one punchline title).

The code lives in `src/reelfactory/story.py` (sets, camera, elements) and `src/reelfactory/cast.py`
(characters and props). A storyboard opts in with `"theme": "story"` and `"type": "story"` scenes; old
`card` storyboards still render exactly as before.

## Layout

```
y    0 ┌──────────────┐
       │  IG top bar  │
  330  │  CAPTIONS    │  kinetic words (keep the stage clear above ~480)
  480  ├──────────────┤
       │    STAGE     │  x 0–1080; slots: far-left 150, left 270, left-third 360,
       │              │  center 540, right-third 720, right 810, far-right 930
 1340  │ ── ground ── │  actors and grounded props stand here by default
 1440  │  labels      │  short tags sit here
 1540  ├──────────────┤  Instagram's UI covers the rest
```

`y` also accepts `top` 600, `sky` 640, `high` 760, `mid` 920, `low` 1120 or `ground`.

## Storyboard shape

```json
{
  "theme": "story",
  "cast": {
    "eko": {"kind": "bot", "color": "accent", "name": "Eko"},
    "researcher": {"kind": "person", "color": "slate", "outfit": ["labcoat", "glasses"]}
  },
  "scenes": [
    {"type": "story", "at": "first words", "params": {
      "set": "island", "transition": "zoom",
      "camera": {"moves": [{"at": "cue", "zoom": 1.25, "focus": "eko", "dur": 0.8}], "shake": [{"at": "cue"}]},
      "title": {"text": "Playing, or *pretending?*", "at": "cue", "out_at": "cue"},
      "elements": [ ... ]
    }}
  ],
  "thumbnail": {"label": "AI experiment", "headline": "Left alone, it *started to play*.",
                "set": "island", "actor": {"who": "eko", "mood": "grin", "pose": "juggle"}}
}
```

Colours can be palette names (`accent`, `slate`, `sage`, `mustard`, `plum`, `sand`, `danger`, `ink`, `muted`)
or hex.

## Timing

Every `at` / `*_at` value is an exact phrase from the script (resolved to the moment it's spoken) or a
number of seconds after the scene starts. Each element:

| key | meaning |
|---|---|
| `at` | when it appears (default: a quick stagger at the start of the scene) |
| `enter` | `pop` · `drop` · `rise` · `grow` · `slam` · `fade` · `walk-left` · `walk-right` · `fly-left` · `fly-right` · `none` |
| `out_at`, `exit` | when it leaves, and how: `pop` · `fade` · `drop` · `walk-left` · `walk-right` |
| `do` | list of changes on cues (below) |
| `id` | name it so swarms, links, confetti and the camera can target it |

A `do` entry is `{"at": cue, ...}` with any of:

- `move`: `[x, y]` (or `{"x":…}`); people walk there, `arc` (px) makes it a jump/throw, `dur` overrides speed
- `pose`, `mood`, `look` (`left` `right` `up` `down` `center`), `say` (speech bubble, ≤ 6 words), `emote`
- `state` (props: `hacked`, `open`, `broken`, `on`, `off`; counters: `struck`)
- numbers that tween: `value` (counters), `level` (meter), `grow` (chart/tower), `size`, `speed`
- `label`, `title`, `text`, `lines`, `color` swap instantly

## Characters (`el: "actor"`, with `who` from `cast`)

- **person**: bean body, face that carries the emotion. Outfits: `hoodie` `glasses` `labcoat` `tie` `suit` `cap` `headset`.
- **bot**: AI agent with a screen face, antenna and hover.
- `size` (person 1.0 ≈ 325 px tall, bot 0.9 ≈ 220 px), `label: true` shows the cast name (or a string).
- `hold`: a prop name drawn in the right hand (e.g. `magnifier`, `phone`, `ball`).
- **Moods**: neutral happy grin smirk sly shock sad worried focused sleepy proud curious angry love
- **Poses**: idle wave cheer point present type hold think shrug relax panic cross juggle throw catch hips sad
  (`point-left`, `wave-left`… mirror them). Poses blend smoothly; `type`, `wave`, `panic`, `juggle` keep moving.
- **Emotes**: `!` `!!` `?` `sparkle` `heart` `zzz` `sweat` `idea` `check` `cross` `music`

## Other elements

| `el` | what it does | key params |
|---|---|---|
| `prop` | an object (list below) | `kind`, `x`, `y`, `size`, `label`, `title`, `lines`, `state`, `glow` |
| `swarm` | agent bots fly from `from` to `to` and get busy there (hopping between grid cells) | `who`, `count` ≤ 40, `from` (id or `[x,y]`), `to` (grid id, element id(s) or points), `stagger`, `size` |
| `grid` | many small icons that turn `fill` colour between `fill_at` and `end_at`, with a live count | `count`, `cols`, `w`, `icon` (site/dot/person), `label`, `fill_to` 0..1 |
| `counter` | big number counting `from`→`to` between `at` and `end_at`; `do` `value` re-sets it | `prefix`, `suffix`, `label`, `font` |
| `label` | short tag (`variant`: tag · plain · big) | `text`, `color`, `arrow` |
| `stamp` | text that slams on with an impact | `text`, `rotate`, `color` |
| `link` | dotted connection with travelling dots | `from`, `to`, `bend`, `color` |
| `crowd` | a row of identical characters popping in | `who`, `count`, `x0`, `x1`, `pose`, `moods` |
| `confetti` | celebration burst | `on` (id) or `x`/`y` |

**Props**: grounded (anchored at their bottom): palm, desk (with laptop), hoop, building, server, mountain,
sign, flag, lamp, block, tower, lava, plant, rock, podium. Floating (anchored at their centre): ball, clock,
note, window, terminal, laptop, bulb, magnifier, lock, shield, trophy, chart, meter, star, phone.

Prop extras: `window`/`terminal` type their `lines` between `at` and `end_at`; `note` highlights line `mark`
at `mark_at`; `chart` takes `bars` [{label, value 0..1}]; `meter` takes `level`; `tower` takes `count`;
`building` shows `label` and flashes red on `state: "hacked"`; `clock` spins at `speed` with a `label`;
`hoop` swishes at `swish_at`.

## Sets, camera, transitions, title

- **Sets**: `stage` (spotlight), `island` (`sky` day/sunset/night, `cycle_at` sweeps day→night, `virtual`, `palm`),
  `night` (stars + soil cross-section), `office`, `lab`, `city`, `cyber`, `room`.
- **Camera**: `zoom`, `focus` (id or `[x,y]`), `drift` (slow push-in, default 0.045), `moves` (keyframes), `shake`.
  Avoid zoom below 1.0 (the set's edges would show).
- **Transition into the scene**: `zoom` (default) · `whip` · `iris` · `fade` · `cut`.
- **Title**: one punchline per Reel at most; while it is on screen the captions step aside.

## Sound

Sound effects follow the action automatically: whoosh on scene changes, swarms, throws and jumps; pop when
things appear; blip for bubbles and emotes; impact for stamps, drops and camera shakes; alert when something
gets hacked. They stay sparse (never two within 0.12 s).

content.text:
The context fix for false alarms is built, tested and pushed (`0fe5dbe`).

**How it works now**

1. **The chat has to back up Ward Lite.** A message only Ward Lite flagged needs support from the chat around it:
   - hurtful words nearby, or
   - the same person being hurtful elsewhere, or
   - the child reacting ("stop", "please", "bas karo", crying).

   Without that, it shows as "I'm not sure about this one" with a dashed outline. It doesn't raise the verdict and doesn't go in a report.
2. **Gemma takes a second look with context.** It re-reads each of those messages with six messages before and two after. I measured whether Gemma can be trusted to clear a flag:

| Gemma | False alarms cleared (good) | Hurtful cleared (bad) | Dangerous cleared (worst) |
|---|---|---|---|
| E4B (computers, Discord host) | 22 of 24 | 2 of 46 | 0 of 12 |
| E2B (phones) | 23 of 24 | 18 of 46 | 1 of 12 |

   So E4B may clear flags. E2B only confirms them: it cleared "no one would even notice if you weren't here tomorrow".
3. **No "looks okay" over a dangerous-sounding message.** When Ward isn't sure about one, the headline says "I'm not sure about one message" and the helplines stay on screen. I checked this in the app.
4. **Discord:** the bot reads the eight messages before anything only Ward Lite flagged. Server mode stays quiet when nothing backs the flag up. Evidence a teen saves needs no context, since choosing it is the backing.

The bot is running again on your Mac with this, using your Ollama Gemma for the second look and with the quiet periods set to 0, so you can test it.

**The animated series:** I found your reel factory at `~/Projects/reel-factory`. It makes about 30-second, 1080×1920 animated story reels with short speech bubbles and timed captions, so each episode is roughly a 70-word script. Two things it will need for Ward:
- **Ward as a character:** there's no ghost character yet, so one needs adding.
- **Roman Urdu captions:** captions are timed by an English-only transcriber today, so that needs a multilingual model or the script itself as captions.

ElevenLabs is out of credits, but the pipeline takes your own recorded voice.

I'll write the Roman Urdu scripts first, as you asked: a social cut for teens and a gentler class cut for kids, which share the episode list. I'm waiting for the audit's episode plan so the series matches its findings.

The audit is checking its last findings. Some touch the new context rule, and I'll go through those with you when the report lands.

For the project owner. I checked every finding below against the code or the docs. Where a first reading was wrong, I used the corrected version. Line numbers refer to the current tree.

---

## 1. Where Ward stands

Ward is unusually good for five days of work. It is also not yet safe to put in front of children at scale. Both are true, and the gap between them is mostly small, fixable work plus a few decisions only you can make.

### What is genuinely strong

- **The safety rules are code, not promises.**
  - Ward Lite can raise a warning but never lower one (`analyze.ts`, `combine()`).
  - When Gemma calls a severity-3 phrase a joke, the message stays visible at severity 2 with "How did it feel?".
  - A child's "This is wrong" can never soften a dangerous message (`corrections.ts:38-44`).
  - All three are pinned by tests (`engine.test.ts:98`, `corrections.test.ts:17`).
- **Privacy engineering is careful.**
  - The Electron window is sandboxed, every IPC call checks its sender, and only the camera permission is allowed (`desktop/main.mjs:46-126`).
  - The vault uses AES-GCM-256 with a fresh IV each time and PBKDF2 at 310k rounds.
  - Android has `allowBackup=false` and FLAG_SECURE.
  - The case viewer runs under `default-src 'none'`, so it cannot make network requests.
- **You publish your failures.**
  - REDTEAM.md says outright that "A child asking for help reads as the bully".
  - The README says "It doesn't solve cyberbullying".
  - DPG.md marks its own indicators "Not yet met".
  - This honesty is your biggest asset with funders, helplines and the DPG Alliance.
- **Evaluation hygiene is better than most production ML.**
  - Leak tests keep the red-team set out of training.
  - Near-duplicate checks protect the scorecard.
  - The "see you tomorrow" shortcut bug was fixed with data, not by tuning against the test. Everyday false alarms fell from 25% to 5%, and urgent results from 16% to 2%.
- **The content is warm and never shames the child.**
  - The "one hour" sextortion story shows that paying never stops it, with no telling-off.
  - Lessons have no hearts to lose.
  - Key strings read at grade 2 to 6.
  - Right-to-left layout is done properly with logical properties, and Urdu is type-checked for parity with English.
- **The engineering holds together.**
  - Strict TypeScript, and a pure engine that runs in browser, Electron, Capacitor and Node.
  - Android CI boots an emulator offline, sends a real WhatsApp share intent, and checks that the "Give Ward" copy is byte-identical.
- **The partner pieces already exist:** ward.report/v2, the offline viewer, the adult guide and a full school kit. A helpline or school pilot needs no new product, only people.

### The five problems that matter most

1. **The safety net has holes exactly where children are most at risk.**
   - On a phone, a lone threat or sextortion demand that only Ward Lite catches is marked "unsure". It never reaches "urgent", the Coach or the report.
   - A calm result has no "this still feels wrong" path to help.
   - Ward never notices the child's own distress.
   - A child quoting abuse to ask for help is read as the bully.
2. **What reaches children is not what was tested.**
   - CI-built APKs and installers ship without ONNX Runtime, so Ward Lite silently doesn't run.
   - The APK won't install on 32-bit budget phones.
   - Every download link and the "Give Ward" QR code lead to a 404, because no release has ever been cut.
   - Saving a chat longer than about 200 messages to the vault fails silently.
3. **Some public claims run ahead of the code.**
   - "Never leaves the device" is false when a phone is paired with a family computer.
   - The report's green "Unchanged since it was saved" can be faked with one line of JavaScript.
   - "Helplines for the child's country" shows Pakistan's numbers to a child in Dubai.
   - The headline scorecard compares a model trained on the test datasets with one that never saw them.
4. **The campaign would outrun your own safeguarding rules.**
   - SAFEGUARDING.md says crisis paths must not be "turned on more widely until the professional review is done".
   - There is no reviewer, no safeguarding lead and no contact inbox.
   - The app currently tells children to post their corrections, optionally with real chat text, to a public GitHub issue.
5. **Discord server mode breaks a public promise.** SAFEGUARDING.md says Ward will never let an adult "receive alerts". Server mode alerts moderators, and it can tell a child who discloses abuse to "edit or delete" their message.
